### 🚨 PR Title Needs Formatting
Please update the title to match our [commit style conventions](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/commit.html).

Errors from script:
```
labels are [t-algebra, new-contributor]
error: the PR title does not contain a colon
```

<details>
<summary>Details on the required title format</summary>

The title should fit the following format:
```
<kind>(<optional-scope>): <subject>
```
`<kind>` is:

- `feat` (feature)
- `fix` (bug fix)
- `doc` (documentation)
- `style` (formatting, missing semicolons, ...)
- `refactor`
- `test` (when adding missing tests)
- `chore` (maintain)
- `perf` (performance improvement, optimization, ...)
- `ci` (changes to continuous integration, repo automation, ...)

`<optional-scope>` is a name of module or a directory which contains changed modules.
This is not necessary to include, but may be useful if the `<subject>` is insufficient.
The `Mathlib` directory prefix is always omitted.
For instance, it could be

- Data/Nat/Basic
- Algebra/Group/Defs
- Topology/Constructions

`<subject>` has the following constraints:

- do not capitalize the first letter
- no dot(.) at the end
- use imperative, present tense: "change" not "changed" nor "changes"
</details>

payload.author: SnirBroshi
payload.body:
Cool! Could you first define the tensor product:
```lean
def tensorProd (G : SimpleGraph α) (H : SimpleGraph β) : SimpleGraph (α × β) :=
  G.comap Prod.fst ⊓ H.comap Prod.snd

infixl:70 " × " => tensorProd

@[simp]
theorem tensorProd_adj {G : SimpleGraph α} {H : SimpleGraph β} {u v : α × β} :
    (G × H).Adj u v ↔ G.Adj u.fst v.fst ∧ H.Adj u.snd v.snd :=
  .rfl
```
and then
```lean
def strongProd (G : SimpleGraph α) (H : SimpleGraph β) : SimpleGraph (α × β) :=
  G □ H ⊔ G × H

infixl:70 " ⊠ " => strongProd

@[simp]
theorem strongProd_adj {G : SimpleGraph α} {H : SimpleGraph β} {u v : α × β} :
    (G ⊠ H).Adj u v ↔ ((G □ H) ⊔ G × H).Adj u v :=
  .rfl

theorem strongProd_adj' {G : SimpleGraph α} {H : SimpleGraph β} {u v : α × β} :
    (G ⊠ H).Adj u v ↔ u ≠ v ∧ (u.1 = v.1 ∨ G.Adj u.1 v.1) ∧ (u.2 = v.2 ∨ H.Adj u.2 v.2) := by
  simp
  grind [Adj.ne]
```

Also could you split the products into separate files? `Prod/Box.lean`, `Prod/Tensor.lean`, `Prod/Strong.lean`
Thanks!

payload.body:
### 🚨 PR Title Needs Formatting
Please update the title to match our [commit style conventions](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/commit.html).

Errors from script:
```
labels are []
error: the PR title does not contain a colon
```

<details>
<summary>Details on the required title format</summary>

The title should fit the following format:
```
<kind>(<optional-scope>): <subject>
```
`<kind>` is:

- `feat` (feature)
- `fix` (bug fix)
- `doc` (documentation)
- `style` (formatting, missing semicolons, ...)
- `refactor`
- `test` (when adding missing tests)
- `chore` (maintain)
- `perf` (performance improvement, optimization, ...)
- `ci` (changes to continuous integration, repo automation, ...)

`<optional-scope>` is a name of module or a directory which contains changed modules.
This is not necessary to include, but may be useful if the `<subject>` is insufficient.
The `Mathlib` directory prefix is always omitted.
For instance, it could be

- Data/Nat/Basic
- Algebra/Group/Defs
- Topology/Constructions

`<subject>` has the following constraints:

- do not capitalize the first letter
- no dot(.) at the end
- use imperative, present tense: "change" not "changed" nor "changes"
</details>
<!-- Sticky Pull Request CommentPR Title Check -->

payload.title: [Merged by Bors] - fix(cache): retry transport errors, improve transfer robustness

payload.author: bryangingechen
payload.body:
A few suggestions from Claude. It also pointed out:
- There is a preexisting bug on the parallel path where truncated files can get renamed. A transport error that outlives the retries reports `http_code: 200` with a nonzero exit code. For example: `http_code = 200`,  `exitcode = 18`,   `errormsg = 'transfer closed with 16 bytes remaining to read'` `size_download = 4`   `(server promised 20)`. `monitorCurl` then matches on `http_code` and renames the 4-byte file to its final `<hash>.ltar` and sends it to `leantar`. This corrupt file never gets re-downloaded unless `.cache` is cleared manually because ` IO.ModuleHashMap.filterExists` only checks `pathExists`. The `%{json}` blob already carries exitcode, so gating the rename on it alongside the status would fix this.
- Pre-existing and adjacent: on a 404 miss `monitorCurl` skips the `removeOnError` branch entirely, so the error-body `.part` file stays in `.cache` (25 bytes in Claude's test). Now asymmetric with the serial path in this PR.
- The probe walk is serial with no `--retry-max-time`: `findRecentSHAsWithCache` is a plain for loop over up to 50 SHAs. With retries and no `--retry-max-time`, a genuinely unreachable endpoint costs ~31s of backoff per probe — `lake exe cache query` goes from failing fast to hanging for ~25 minutes offline. `informIfHeadNotBuilt` adds ~31s before every fork `cache get`. The download paths are much less exposed: the parallel path is bounded by `--parallel`, and the "serial" path actually spawns every `downloadFile` as a concurrent `IO.asTask`.

payload.author: bryangingechen
payload.body:
Two minor comments and one more substantial one:

> The --retry-max-time 30 on the probe doesn't bound anything. curl checks the retry timer before starting an attempt and doesn't cut the backoff sleep before it, so with the default 1/2/4/8/16 schedule attempts begin at t = 0, 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 — and 30 is exactly the value where the bound never binds. Measured with curl 8.7.1 against a DNS failure: master's probe 0.014s, this branch 31s (33s against a blackholed IP). --connect-timeout/--max-time are free and worth keeping; the cost is --retry alone. Worth noting for local testing that connection-refused isn't retried, so a closed local port returns instantly — you need a DNS failure or dropped packets to see it.
>
> The multiplier is the bigger half: probeContainerForSHA collapses exitCode != 0 into false, so a transport error is indistinguishable from "no marker" and findRecentSHAsWithCache has no way to stop. Offline that's 50 × 31s ≈ 26 min for cache query and discoverUnsafeScopes, plus 31s in informIfHeadNotBuilt before every default fork cache get.
>
> Two directions, either or both: the probe is diagnostic and a false negative is cheap (unlike the download paths, where retry is clearly right), so it may not want --retry at all; and letting the walk bail on the first transport error fixes the ×50 rather than the constant. The second also makes cache query's "This usually means CI hasn't built any of these commits yet" honest — offline it currently prints that, after 26 minutes, when the real cause is no network.

<details>
<summary>Details on the required title format</summary>

The title should fit the following format:
```
<kind>(<optional-scope>): <subject>
```
`<kind>` is:

- `feat` (feature)
- `fix` (bug fix)
- `doc` (documentation)
- `style` (formatting, missing semicolons, ...)
- `refactor`
- `test` (when adding missing tests)
- `chore` (maintain)
- `perf` (performance improvement, optimization, ...)
- `ci` (changes to continuous integration, repo automation, ...)

`<optional-scope>` is a name of module or a directory which contains changed modules.
This is not necessary to include, but may be useful if the `<subject>` is insufficient.
The `Mathlib` directory prefix is always omitted.
For instance, it could be

- Data/Nat/Basic
- Algebra/Group/Defs
- Topology/Constructions

`<subject>` has the following constraints:

- do not capitalize the first letter
- no dot(.) at the end
- use imperative, present tense: "change" not "changed" nor "changes"

I do actually think the import increase is a big deal. The idea is that this file will define the `ZeroDimensionalSpace` predicate, which is a unified spelling for the "has a basis of clopen sets" predicate which does appear in files with relatively restricted imports.

What about making an `InductiveDimension` folder? Then the current material can be moved to`Defs`, and perhaps this new material can go in a `Real` flie.

payload.author: felixpernegger
payload.body:
Yeah good point.
There is also Mathlib/Topology/Instances/Real/Lemmas.lean where this could be maybe, but eventually we need a subfolder

Please update the title to match our [commit style conventions](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/commit.html).

<details>
<summary>Details on the required title format</summary>

The title should fit the following format:
```
<kind>(<optional-scope>): <subject>
```
`<kind>` is:

- `feat` (feature)
- `fix` (bug fix)
- `doc` (documentation)
- `style` (formatting, missing semicolons, ...)
- `refactor`
- `test` (when adding missing tests)
- `chore` (maintain)
- `perf` (performance improvement, optimization, ...)
- `ci` (changes to continuous integration, repo automation, ...)

`<optional-scope>` is a name of module or a directory which contains changed modules.
This is not necessary to include, but may be useful if the `<subject>` is insufficient.
The `Mathlib` directory prefix is always omitted.
For instance, it could be

- Data/Nat/Basic
- Algebra/Group/Defs
- Topology/Constructions

`<subject>` has the following constraints:

- do not capitalize the first letter
- no dot(.) at the end
- use imperative, present tense: "change" not "changed" nor "changes"

payload.body: Should I be concerned about the import increases in `Mathlib.Tactic.Echelon.Parsing` or `Mathlib.Tactic.Echelon.Zsqrtd`?

payload.author: grunweg
payload.body: What do you think, @bryangingechen?

payload.author: kbuzzard
payload.body: More generally, how can shaking make imports go up in a file?

payload.author: bryangingechen
payload.body:
Regarding changes in `Tactic.Echelon.*`; these are new files that were added in #42652, so I'm not too surprised that there are some changes there. 

> More generally, how can shaking make imports go up in a file?

There are two obvious ways `shake` can give rise to import "increases":
- shake tells us to import some of `A.lean`'s imports `B.lean`, `C.lean` and `D.lean` instead of just `A.lean`.
- if shake was able to reduce the imports of `A.lean`, they might need to be added back in downstream files. 

<details><summary>Some explicit examples from Claude</summary>
An example of the first is apparently [`Tactic/Echelon/Parsing.lean`](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/43073/changes#diff-cd5dc4a7679a8c5f19e0beb52e5a2d134c4f16a6dc744977be01fcad764337c6) where `shake` dropped `LinearAlgebra.Matrix.Notation` and added 8 more specific imports.

Two examples of the second:
  - `Order/Cover.lean` removes `Order.Hom.WithTopBot` → `CategoryTheory/Presentable/CardinalDirectedPoset.lean` (downstream of Cover) adds it back.
  - `WalkingPair.lean` drops `Comma.Over.Basic`, `EpiMono`, `Shapes.Terminal` → `BinaryFan.lean` adds `HasLimits` + `IsTerminal` → `BinaryProducts.lean` adds back `Comma.Over.Basic` + `Shapes.Terminal`.
</details>

According to Claude, these account for 22 of the 42 import additions. The other 20 come from these two more subtle changes:
- A module that declares a `aesop` rule sets or register some attributes (including `norm_num`, `positivity` and `bareiss_ext`) records "reverse use" flags using `Lean.recordExtraRevUseOfCurrentModule` and `shake` forces modules that transitively depends on this module to name it explicitly. This is a safe overapproximation that prevents `shake` from removing imports that would break uses of these attributes. The attributes mostly do have related TODOs here, so maybe these will be fixed at some point, cf. [this one in `Tactic.NormNum.Core`](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/master/Mathlib/Tactic/NormNum/Core.lean#L204).
- Sometimes a module is needed both during elaboration and compile time (e.g. `public import Mathlib.NumberTheory.Zsqrtd.Basic ` and `public meta import Mathlib.NumberTheory.Zsqrtd.Basic` in `Echelon/Zsqrtd.lean`); `shake` makes this explicit.

## Pull request overview Adds affine-geometric support for expressing simplex cross-sections perpendicular to an altitude as shifted opposite faces. **Changes:** - Adds orthogonal-complement lemmas for linear isometries and relative submodules. - Adds membership lemmas for shifted affine subspaces. - Proves the simplex altitude cross-section identities. ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 6 out of 6 changed files in this pull request and generated no comments.
Show a summary per file | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | `Mathlib/Analysis/InnerProductSpace/Orthogonal.lean` | Adds orthogonal-complement map/comap identities. | | `Mathlib/Analysis/InnerProductSpace/Projection/Basic.lean` | Transfers orthogonal projections through isometric comaps. | | `Mathlib/Analysis/InnerProductSpace/Projection/Submodule.lean` | Proves relative orthogonal complementation is involutive. | | `Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/AffineSpace/AffineSubspace/Defs.lean` | Adjusts affine-infimum coercion notation. | | `Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/AffineSpace/AffineSubspace/Shift.lean` | Adds shifted-subspace membership lemmas. | | `Mathlib/Geometry/Euclidean/Altitude.lean` | Establishes the perpendicular cross-section identities. |

payload.author: SnirBroshi
payload.body:
Welcome!

Could you elaborate on the choice of junk values, and add the reasons behind them to the module docstring?

About the name: we have `Nat.minFac`, so should this be called `maxFac`? or should we rename `minFac` to `minPrimeFac`? and maybe even expand the awkward "factor" abbrevation?

Also could you trim the description please? It looks AI generated and is a bit verbose.

payload.author: bocowgill
payload.body: Thanks for the review. I renamed the definition to `Nat.maxFac` to match `Nat.minFac`, documented the exceptional values and their rationale, and trimmed the PR description. Renaming `minFac` or expanding `Fac` seems like a broader API change, so I left that for a separate PR, but I’m happy to follow up if useful.

payload.author: SnirBroshi
payload.body:
Thanks! I prefer `Nat.maxPrimeFactor` but that should probably be discussed on Zulip.

About the junk values: Your explanation says that `maxFac n ≤ n` always holds and says that `maxFac 0 = 0` is chosed for the `sSup` lemma, but the `sSup` lemma assumes `n ≠ 1` so wouldn't this mean `maxFac 1 = 0` is a better choice by that reasoning, so that the `sSup` lemma would hold everywhere? Although then `maxFac n ∣ n` won't.

You also mention that `maxFac 1 = 1` "makes the multiplicative identity a fixed point". What does this mean exactly? It's a true statement, but why is it something we want?

payload.author: YaelDillies
payload.body:
A minimal factor of a natural number is always a prime number when it exists. A maximal factor of a natural  number is always the natural number divided by some prime number. Therefore having the two definitions be called `minFac` and `maxPrimeFac` seems totally reasonable to me.

Please change the name back, as `maxFac` is mathematically incorrect as a name.

payload.author: SnirBroshi
payload.body:
> We instead care about the `IsLeast` one, and no value of `maxPrimeFac` will make that one true at `n = 1`

If you're referring to `isLeast_maxFac`, then `maxPrimeFac 1 = 0` will make it true at `n = 1`.

There's no other `IsLeast` lemma in the PR; did you perhaps mean `IsGreatest n.primeFactors n.maxPrimeFac` rather than `IsLeast`, or am I missing something?

payload.author: YaelDillies
payload.body: No sorry, you are right, it would hold at `n = 1`. I still prefer the junk value of `maxPrimeFac 1 = 1`, because divisibility feels more important than LUBness, but I am not fussed

payload.author: SnirBroshi
payload.body:
> divisibility feels more important than LUBness

I agree, but then what's the reason for `maxPrimeFac 0 = 0` rather than 1 or 2? Both preserve divisibility. I guess only 0 allows for `n.maxPrimeFac ≤ n` but that seems arbitrary.
Regardless, I think the reasoning should be documented in the module docstring.

payload.author: bocowgill
payload.body:
> > divisibility feels more important than LUBness
> 
> I agree, but then what's the reason for `maxPrimeFac 0 = 0` rather than 1 or 2? Both preserve divisibility. I guess only 0 allows for `n.maxPrimeFac ≤ n` but that seems arbitrary. Regardless, I think the reasoning should be documented in the module docstring.

The two laws pin both values down if you take them together: `∣ n` is vacuous at `0` but forces `1` at `n = 1`, and `≤ n` forces `0` at `n = 0` but allows either at `n = 1`. So it's one rule — return `n` when the factor list is empty — rather than two independent choices, which is what `getLastD n` gives.

I'll document that, along with the `IsLUB`/divisibility tradeoff at `1`, and drop the "fixed point" line since it wasn't really an argument.

payload.author: bocowgill
payload.body: Separately, I started a Zulip thread on `maxPrimeFac` vs `maxPrimeFactor` [here](https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/287929-mathlib4/topic/PR.20.2343034.3A.20maxPrimeFac.20vs.20maxPrimeFactor/near/618125511). No replies yet. Either way I'll restore a prime-specific name per Yael's point. Absent a preference for the longer spelling I'll go with `maxPrimeFac`.

payload.author: bocowgill
payload.body:
7e73cc3ad6 is up and CI is green. This supersedes my earlier reply about `maxFac` — the name is now `Nat.maxPrimeFac`, per Yael's point that the maximal factor of `n` is `n` itself. Still no replies on the Zulip thread about the longer spelling; happy to rename if one appears.

The module docstring now carries the junk-value reasoning, including the `IsLUB`/divisibility tradeoff at `1`.

payload.author: dennj
payload.body:
> Which type is being abused here? Do you know?

It's not ToType. The aesop call fails without the flag even for a generic f : ι → β, so it's the subtype ↥(Set.range f): aesop needs to unfold · ∈ Set.range f inside the type to close the goal, and the flag allows that. The explicit rintro proof doesn't touch the type, so the flag can go.

payload.author: YaelDillies
payload.body: Ideally we would like `aesop` to work here, even without the flag. Could you investigate what lemmas/annotations are missing to make it work?

payload.author: dennj
payload.body:
> Ideally we would like `aesop` to work here, even without the flag. Could you investigate what lemmas/annotations are missing to make it work?

Nothing is missing from aesop: the problem was the term `⟨f i, i, rfl⟩` itself. Its membership proof has type ∃ y, f y = f i and using it as f i ∈ Set.range f is exactly the defeq the flag re-allowed; since that sits inside the Subtype.mk, the Subtype.mk.injEq step aesop wants to use fails to typecheck without the flag. Writing `⟨f i, Set.mem_range_self i⟩` instead makes plain aesop work with no flag and no extra lemmas, so the diff is now just the set_option removal plus that one term fix.

payload.body:
### 🚨 PR Title Needs Formatting
Please update the title to match our [commit style conventions](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/commit.html).

Errors from script:
```
labels are [t-measure-probability]
error: a PR's scope must not contain spaces
```

<details>
<summary>Details on the required title format</summary>

The title should fit the following format:
```
<kind>(<optional-scope>): <subject>
```
`<kind>` is:

- `feat` (feature)
- `fix` (bug fix)
- `doc` (documentation)
- `style` (formatting, missing semicolons, ...)
- `refactor`
- `test` (when adding missing tests)
- `chore` (maintain)
- `perf` (performance improvement, optimization, ...)
- `ci` (changes to continuous integration, repo automation, ...)

`<optional-scope>` is a name of module or a directory which contains changed modules.
This is not necessary to include, but may be useful if the `<subject>` is insufficient.
The `Mathlib` directory prefix is always omitted.
For instance, it could be

- Data/Nat/Basic
- Algebra/Group/Defs
- Topology/Constructions

`<subject>` has the following constraints:

- do not capitalize the first letter
- no dot(.) at the end
- use imperative, present tense: "change" not "changed" nor "changes"
</details>
<!-- Sticky Pull Request CommentPR Title Check -->

payload.body: Great minds think alike, it seems; I had a similar PR in the works at #42940.

payload.author: loefflerd
payload.body: It looks like your split is slightly more "fine-grained" than mine (8 pieces rather than 5). But are you sure it's a good idea to move to non-public imports at the same time? It seems orthogonal to the file-splitting; and I don't think there's a settled consensus yet on which imports should be public and which not.

payload.author: EtienneC30
payload.body:
Haha yes it's funny I've had it in mind for some time and decided to tackle it today 😅
Indeed mine is finer, I thought it wouldn't hurt. Regarding `public`, I agree it is orthogonal but I also thought that it was a good time to do it. From my understanding if a file can be imported non-publicly then it should.

payload.author: loefflerd
payload.body:
> Regarding public, I agree it is orthogonal but I also thought that it was a good time to do it. From my understanding if a file can be imported non-publicly then it should.

I'm not sure I understand this argument: any file *can* be imported non-publicly if you are willing to add imports in downstream files (as you have done – that is why your PR touches 90 files while mine only touches 10). So applying your criterion across mathlib would end up with making every single import private, at a cost of some files probably ending up with more import lines than actual code lines.

payload.author: EtienneC30
payload.body: No because if your file contains a definition that appears in a statement or an exposed definition you have to import it publicly.

payload.author: EtienneC30
payload.body: Also you would have at most one import by declaration you use in the file (much less in reality), so I am not sure it would lead to that much import.

payload.author: dennj
payload.body:
> vihdzp

This PR is me following up on Yaël's suggestion in #40725, after my attempt to deprecate ToType outright was pushed back on.

ToType becomes an abbrev of a library type, so LinearOrder/WellFoundedLT and ToType.mk (now literally orderIsoShrink) come from Order/Shrink instead of being hand-rolled from o.out, and small_Iio no longer goes through ToType. What it costs is visible in this diff too: as an abbrev, Shrink instances leak through (hence the priority := 50 in EssentiallySmall and the IsCardinalFiltered tweak).

I don't have a strong opinion on how ToType is defined. My original motivation was only that it should be used less. So @YaelDillies @vihdzp, could you two agree on a direction?

payload.author: vihdzp
payload.body: Ah, getting the instances for free is actually a really nice application of this! I can agree on this.

payload.body:
### 🚨 PR Title Needs Formatting
Please update the title to match our [commit style conventions](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/commit.html).

Errors from script:
```
labels are []
error: the PR title does not contain a colon
```

<details>
<summary>Details on the required title format</summary>

The title should fit the following format:
```
<kind>(<optional-scope>): <subject>
```
`<kind>` is:

- `feat` (feature)
- `fix` (bug fix)
- `doc` (documentation)
- `style` (formatting, missing semicolons, ...)
- `refactor`
- `test` (when adding missing tests)
- `chore` (maintain)
- `perf` (performance improvement, optimization, ...)
- `ci` (changes to continuous integration, repo automation, ...)

`<optional-scope>` is a name of module or a directory which contains changed modules.
This is not necessary to include, but may be useful if the `<subject>` is insufficient.
The `Mathlib` directory prefix is always omitted.
For instance, it could be

- Data/Nat/Basic
- Algebra/Group/Defs
- Topology/Constructions

`<subject>` has the following constraints:

- do not capitalize the first letter
- no dot(.) at the end
- use imperative, present tense: "change" not "changed" nor "changes"
</details>
<!-- Sticky Pull Request CommentPR Title Check -->

> The name change does make sense to me, but for the theorem you want to prove you should instead write:

Ah sorry, yes, reading again now I realize the initial description wasn't clear enough --- said more clearly, the theorem (often called Alexandrov's theorem in Descriptive Set Theory circles) is: given a metrizable space S, any completely metrizable subspace s is Gdelta as a subset of X. FWIW that is up now as a PR #42912

payload.author: Vierkantor
payload.body:
I am leaning towards agreeing with your idea that this linter should only fire on constructors imported from other modules. That most closely matches the behaviour of the original private constructor design idea, and setting up a public wrapper in the same file where the internal constructor is defined seems fine.

Implementation looks nice and straightforward. Doing it as an InfoTree linter makes sure we complain about user-written code (so someone could implement some macros around private constructors without running into big issues).

+0.8% is a bit of a big performance hit for a relatively simple linter, so I had an idea to speed it up, potentially.

payload.body:
### 🚨 PR Title Needs Formatting
Please update the title to match our [commit style conventions](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/commit.html).

Errors from script:
```
labels are []
error: the PR title should be of the form
  kind: subject
or
  kind(scope): subject
Allowed values for `kind` are [feat, chore, perf, refactor, style, fix, doc, test, ci]
```

<details>
<summary>Details on the required title format</summary>

The title should fit the following format:
```
<kind>(<optional-scope>): <subject>
```
`<kind>` is:

- `feat` (feature)
- `fix` (bug fix)
- `doc` (documentation)
- `style` (formatting, missing semicolons, ...)
- `refactor`
- `test` (when adding missing tests)
- `chore` (maintain)
- `perf` (performance improvement, optimization, ...)
- `ci` (changes to continuous integration, repo automation, ...)

`<optional-scope>` is a name of module or a directory which contains changed modules.
This is not necessary to include, but may be useful if the `<subject>` is insufficient.
The `Mathlib` directory prefix is always omitted.
For instance, it could be

- Data/Nat/Basic
- Algebra/Group/Defs
- Topology/Constructions

`<subject>` has the following constraints:

- do not capitalize the first letter
- no dot(.) at the end
- use imperative, present tense: "change" not "changed" nor "changes"
</details>

payload.body:
This is better:
```lean
theorem imo2019_q4 {k n : ℕ} (hk : 0 < k) (hn : 0 < n) :
    (k ! : ℤ) = ∏ i ∈ range n, ((2 : ℤ) ^ n - (2 : ℤ) ^ i) ↔ (k, n) = (1, 1) ∨ (k, n) = (3, 2) := by
  -- The implication `←` holds.
  constructor
  swap
  · rintro (h | h) <;> rcases Prod.ext_iff.mp h with ⟨rfl, rfl⟩ <;> decide
  intro h
  -- We know that n < 6.
  have := Imo2019Q4.upper_bound hk h
  interval_cases n <;>
  simp_rw [prod_range_succ, prod_range_zero, Int.reducePow, Int.reduceSub] at h <;> norm_cast at h
  -- n = 1
  · rw [mul_one, factorial_eq_one] at h
    simp [le_antisymm h hk]
  -- n = 2
  · right; congr; rwa [← factorial_inj' (by lia)]
  -- n = 3
  · refine absurd h (monotone_factorial.ne_of_lt_of_lt_nat 5 ?_ ?_ _) <;> decide
  -- n = 4
  · refine absurd h (monotone_factorial.ne_of_lt_of_lt_nat 7 ?_ ?_ _) <;> decide
  -- n = 5
  · refine absurd h (monotone_factorial.ne_of_lt_of_lt_nat 10 ?_ ?_ _) <;> decide
```

payload.author: joneugster
payload.body:
Thanks for the PR! Overall I think this is already in quite good shape. Two things I've noticed, which are also mentioned above:

- it would be good to have more documentation, maybe also relating the tactic to other, existing tactics (i.e. when should I use `linarith` when `dyadic_interval` when talking about inequalities on reals?)
- I've noticed that recently newer tactics tend to have quite a lot of API localised to the tactic's folder. I think it would be desirable to think about which parts make sense to be generic (public) API, so that the tactic itself remains slicker. In this case it seems to be mainly the theory about `Dyadics` and `Intervals`, see question above

(for context: I've done only a superficial review with focus on maintainability, so there might be the need for a more detailed one in the future)

payload.author: SnirBroshi
payload.body:
Welcome!

It looks like this PR defines a matrix, shows that it's row stochastic, and that's it for now. What are your plans for this def? Could you include a nontrivial result in this PR?

Isn't this stuck without first developing some theory for Markov chains in `MeasureTheory/`?

payload.author: than4213
payload.body:
Thanks for the review!

I was opting to keep the PR small for ease of review.  But you're right that it needed a substantive result to justify itself.  So I've added the stationary distribution: `degreeDist v = deg(v) / 2|E|`, with a proof that it's fixed by the transition matrix.

What are your plans for this def? I just think that probability distributions over spaces defined by graphs is an interesting problem and the random walk is a good first step in that exploration.  I plan to develop this with stuff like Reversibility `π v * P v w = π w * P w v` in the future.

On Markov chain theory in MeasureTheory/ — I don't think we are there yet. The results here are finite sums over ℚ. Reversibility is similarly elementary, and n-step distributions are just `M ^ n`. We can deal with Measure when we take on limiting behaviour, but that's downstream.

Related: #34713 adds IsStationary for general stochastic matrices. If that lands, this could be restated in those terms, though I've kept them independent for now.

payload.author: SnirBroshi
payload.body:
> But you're right that it needed a substantive result to justify itself. So I've added the stationary distribution

It would be cool if we had some Markov chain stuff to link it to, but right now all you have here is some matrix and some vector, and you've shown `vM = v`.

payload.author: than4213
payload.body:
Doesn't `rowStochastic Q V` demonstrated in `walkMatrix_mem_rowStochastic` already establish that it is a Markov chain?  It seems like membership in rowStochastic satisfies the 3 requirements of Markov chains, namely:
1) Square matrix (V applies to rows and columns)
2) non-negative entries
3) rows summing to one

From what it looks like to me the home of rowStochastic (`LinearAlgebra/Matrix/Stochastic.lean`) is the proper home of Markov chains and I feel it is unfortunate that there isn't a more explicit reference to Markov chains there.

In the rest of the file, I intend to establish properties that don't necessarily follow from rowStochastic, like the fact that its distribution is stationary (vM = v for v = degreeDist).  I wanted the PR to be small, but I'm willing to add more theorems, like reversibility.  Do you think this is necessary to justify the value of the PR?

payload.author: wwylele
payload.body:
Thanks for the suggestion! I have rewritten the PR to make the theorem applicable to all `[ContinuousEvalConst F α β]
  [IsMulApply F α β] [IsOneApply F α β]`. As for renaming the existing `tprod_apply`, I chose to do the rename + new version in one go, as the breakage isn't large. It would be awkward to introduce a deprecation notice for old `tprod_apply`, then immediately remove it in the next PR.

Thanks for doing this! This broadly looks good to me; I have two kinds of minor comments:
- when renaming a theorem, the standard procedure is to use a deprecated `alias` instead of copy-pasting the theorem. Please use that (unless there is a specific reason this cannot work; I don't see one immediately), i.e. write something like
```
@[deprecated (since := "2026-08-17")]
alias old_name := new_name
``` 
- the diff makes me realize there are many more misnamed lemmas like so. Would you like to rename some of them also? (If so, this would make a great follow-up PR, or several.)

Do you have a plan on including the generalization in the other PR about the open embedding constructor for IsLinearTopology? Or the open embedding nature of the algebraMap?

payload.author: joneugster
payload.body:
Welcome, and thanks for the PR!

I suggest to start by introducing and discussing the project on [Zulip](https://leanprover.zulipchat.com) and/or link relevant Zulip topics here in the PR description for quick access. It is probably beyond the competence of a single reviewer to add featured projects, but I'll pass this PR on to the maintainer team.

By the look of things, the mentioned repository has been created on May 8 this year, which is quiet recent. There might be a chance that this PR might be deferred for a bit to allow some.

(btw, off-topic: your paper mentions a "verification-gate" using only `grep` and `#print axioms`. This is has significant shortcomings and can fairly easily be circumvented by a rouge actor using hacky meta-code. You should look into something like [comparator](https://github.com/leanprover/comparator/) if you want more assertion; see also https://comparator.live.lean-lang.org)

payload.author: ADedecker
payload.body:
Here is a suggestion, which you should feel free to discard as too much work: I think we should already change the definition of `HasSummableGeomSeries` to work in the non-unital case, by using your `iterate` spelling for powers in non-unital rings.

The rationale is that, even if we wait for `PNat` powers to land, we will have to do much of this refactor; crucially, we will have to provide API in the unital case to get back to the more obvious spelling with the sum starting at zero. So even if we use a slightly weird definition for now, I think it would be a step in the correct direction, and the final refactor to use `PNat` powers would then become relatively trivial.

What do you think?

payload.author: themathqueen
payload.body:
I agree with Anatole here. Except I think the definition should maybe change to `∀ x : A, ‖x‖ < 1 → IsQuasiregular x` and then have a lemma showing the equivalence between that and the iterate spelling summable thing.
But then "HasSummableGeomSeries" might be confusing if the definition is about `IsQuasiregular`. So maybe not. Hmm.

payload.author: ADedecker
payload.body: Aha, it did not occur to me that these would be equivalent. It is indeed worth thinking about which spelling is the best (and if we end up switching to an invertibility statement, probably the name should change as well).

payload.author: j-loreaux
payload.body:
> I agree with Anatole here. Except I think the definition should maybe change to `∀ x : A, ‖x‖ < 1 → IsQuasiregular x` and then have a lemma showing the equivalence between that and the iterate spelling summable thing.
> But then "HasSummableGeomSeries" might be confusing if the definition is about `IsQuasiregular`. So maybe not. Hmm.

I'll open another PR which changes the definition of `HasSummableGeomSeries`. I think we should keep the definition in terms of summability (so that random passersby don't need to go hunt wtf `IsQuasiregular` means, as it won't matter to most people), but I'll provide `↔` statements for the equivalences.

payload.author: j-loreaux
payload.body:
We should probably also have these for `ClosedSubmodule` since we duplicate lemmas. You can copy these into the right place.

```lean
/-- `v ∈ Kᗮ` if and only if `re ⟪u, v⟫ = 0` for all `u ∈ K`; it suffices to check only the
real part of the inner product is zero. -/
lemma mem_orthogonal_iff_re_inner_eq_zero {v : E} :
    v ∈ Kᗮ ↔ ∀ u ∈ K, RCLike.re ⟪u, v⟫ = 0 :=
  K.toSubmodule.mem_orthogonal_iff_re_inner_eq_zero

/-- `v ∈ Kᗮ` if and only if `re ⟪u, v⟫ = 0` for all `u ∈ K`; it suffices to check only the
real part of the inner product is zero. Variation of `mem_orthogonal_iff_re_inner_eq_zero` with
the inner product reversed. -/
lemma mem_orthogonal_iff_re_inner_eq_zero' {v : E} :
    v ∈ Kᗮ ↔ ∀ u ∈ K, RCLike.re ⟪v, u⟫ = 0 :=
  K.toSubmodule.mem_orthogonal_iff_re_inner_eq_zero'
```

payload.author: j-loreaux
payload.body:
This is a useful enough lemma that I think we can add it (in `InnerProductSpace/Basic.lean`.
```lean
/-- `⟪x, y⟫ = 0` if and only if `re ⟪c • x, y⟫ = 0` for every `c : 𝕜` -/
theorem inner_eq_zero_iff_forall_re_inner_smul_left {x y : E} :
    ⟪x, y⟫ = 0 ↔ ∀ c : 𝕜, re ⟪c • x, y⟫ = 0 := by
  refine ⟨fun h c ↦ by simp [inner_smul_left, h], fun h ↦ ?_⟩
  simpa [inner_smul_left, RCLike.conj_mul, -inner_conj_symm] using h ⟪x, y⟫
```
You can also use this to golf the proof of `norm_eq_iInf_iff_inner_eq_zero`:
```diff
-    apply RCLike.ext
-    · simp [A w hw]
-    · symm
-      calc
-        im (0 : 𝕜) = 0 := im.map_zero
-        _ = re ⟪u - v, (-I : 𝕜) • w⟫ := (A _ (K.smul_mem (-I) hw)).symm
-        _ = re (-I * ⟪u - v, w⟫) := by rw [inner_smul_right]
-        _ = im ⟪u - v, w⟫ := by simp
+    rw [inner_eq_zero_symm]
+    exact inner_eq_zero_iff_forall_re_inner_smul_left.2 fun c ↦
+      (inner_re_symm _ _).trans (A _ (K.smul_mem c hw))
```
although probably that last line is better as a `by rw [inner_re_symm, A _ (K.smul_mem c hw]`

payload.author: JovanGerb
payload.body:
> strange interaction of `to_dual` with `simps`/`implicit_reducible` attributes

What is going on is that there are 3 times at which attributes can be added: `beforeElaboration`, `afterTypeChecking` and `afterCompilation`. These happen at these 3 different times, so they happen in this order. `implicit_reducible` is `afterTypeChecking`, while `simps` is `afterCompilation`, so `implicit_reducible` automatically runs first. However, `to_dual` has to apply all attributes at the same time, so it doesn't respect this order. I should make it so that the attributes in `to_dual` are reordered based on their application time.

payload.body: ## Pull request overview This PR introduces the Complex Bessel function of the first kind `Complex.besselJ` via the regularized hypergeometric function infrastructure, and wires the new file into the Mathlib import tree. **Changes:** - Add `Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Bessel.lean` defining `Complex.besselJ` and basic symmetry/analyticity lemmas. - Add a `[simp]` lemma specializing the convergence radius of `regularizedHGFunSeries 0 b` to `⊤`, simplifying analyticity proofs using the power series API. - Import the new Bessel file from `Mathlib.lean`. ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 3 out of 3 changed files in this pull request and generated 2 comments. | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/RegularizedHypergeometric.lean | Adds a simp lemma for radius = ⊤ in the `a = 0` case to streamline downstream analyticity arguments. | | Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Bessel.lean | New file defining `Complex.besselJ` and initial properties (parity for integer order, analyticity statements, value at 0). | | Mathlib.lean | Exposes the new Bessel development through the main Mathlib import surface. | --- 💡 Add a `code-review` agent skill or configure MCP servers for context-aware, tailored reviews. payload.author: mcdoll
payload.body:
Thanks! I think this is a good size, Bessel functions are obviously an important object to have in mathlib and this provides the basic facts. A few minor comments below.

I have a few major points:
The docstrings contain a lot of LaTeX code which often does not seem necessary. Also the docstring for `besselJ` is overly long and I think parts of it should be in the module docstring, not in the docstring for the definition.

Most proofs are pretty short which is great, but `besselJ_neg_int` is a bit lengthy and I think there should be a fact about 0F1 proved here. It does not feel right to do things like unfolding `regularizedHGFun` here, that should only be done in the file for the hypergeometric function. The reason is that if one wants to define the modified Bessel function, then a similar identity should be true (I haven't checked what it is exactly), and the modified Bessel function is also defined in terms of 0F1, so this would lead to code duplication.

payload.author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer
payload.body:
## Pull request overview

Copilot reviewed 3 out of 3 changed files in this pull request and generated no new comments.




<details>
<summary>Suppressed comments (4)</summary>

**Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Bessel.lean:71**
* `slitPlane` excludes the nonpositive real axis, including zero, so “negative real axis” overstates the domain proved by this theorem. Use “nonpositive” to match the hypothesis.
```
/-- $J_a(x)$ is analytic outside of the branch cut on the negative real axis. -/
```
**Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/RegularizedHypergeometric.lean:259**
* These theorem names refer to `regularizedHGFunSeries`, but both conclusions establish analyticity of `regularizedHGFun`. This makes the new public API misleading and prevents users from finding these lemmas under the function's name. Rename both lemmas and the internal reference accordingly.
```
theorem analyticAt_regularizedHGFunSeries_of_card_le (h : a.card ≤ b.card) (x : ℂ) :
```
**Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Bessel.lean:19**
* This paragraph overgeneralizes the branch behavior to all Bessel functions: integer-order Bessel functions of the second kind still have a branch cut, whereas the no-branch-cut statement proved here applies specifically to `besselJ`. Scope the statement to the first-kind function introduced by this file.

This issue also appears on line 71 of the same file.
```
We introduce Bessel functions in this file. Bessel functions commonly take two complex parameter
`a` and `x`. It is analytic for `x ∈ Complex.slitPlane`. For integer `a`, this branch cut vanishes
and it is analytic for all `x`, except for possibly a pole at `x = 0` for some Bessel functions.
```
**Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Bessel.lean:32**
* The comma incorrectly joins two independent sentences, and `For` should not be capitalized after it.
```
$J_a(0) = 0$ for all complex $a \ne 0$, For $a = 0$, we have $J_0(0) = 1$.
```
</details>

payload.author: j-loreaux
payload.body:
Okay, there is a lot of boilerplate here, you are correct about that, but I think there are several things I would like to see and room for major improvement.

0. Before anything, we should decide whether to use `ℂ ⊗[ℝ] E` or `E × E` as the type backing this. I am tempted to agree that `E × E` is the correct choice, because we will so often want to access the real and imaginary parts, but it should come with a detailed `## Implementation Notes` section in the module documentation justifying the choice.
1. As indicated in a comment below, use `E × E` instead of `WithLp 2 (E × E)` so we can reuse `Complexification` for C⋆-algebras (and maybe other things?)
2. Please, please, let's add some scoped notation for this if we can come up with a good one.
3. Let's drop the `𝕜` parameter
4. Due to (1) split out all the norm material from the module material.
5. I would like to see this split into at least three, but maybe closer to 5 PRs as follows:

  - module structure (and even star algebra structures) and basic API
  - norm properties of `WithLp 2 (Complexification E)`
  - properties specific to complexification of spaces involving continuous linear maps
  - connection to tensor products

I'll certainly have more to say later, but I think I've given you enough to chew on.

payload.body:
@ADedecker, so this is a huge PR, but would you like to take a look? 🙏
Take your time of course.
Most of the code is just really basic API, which is why it's long.
I can split out the `TensorProduct` file into another PR, but thought it could be nice to have the equivalence `Complexification 𝕜 E ≃ₗ[ℂ] ℂ ⊗[ℝ] E` in this PR, since that's another way of defining this.

payload.author: ADedecker
payload.body:
Argh, I forgot that I was pinged here, and I had important comments to make, sorry.

We discussed this a bit with Jireh and Filippo at ICERM, and I think I disagree with a key design choice: when `E` is a complex vector space, I think `Complexification ℂ E` should be (complex-isomorphic to) `E`; if you really want to complexify the underlying real vector space then you should simply use `Complexification ℝ E`. This works out of the box if you use the "tensoring with ℂ over 𝕜 definition" (at least mathematically).

Now, one issue with our approach is that we don't know that `ℂ` is a `𝕜`-algebra for RCLike `𝕜`, and that we can't write such an instance without creating bad diamonds; I think we ended up agreeing that we should have a type alias `RCLike.complexField` for `ℂ` viewed as a `𝕜`-algebra, but I'm still not 100% sure what things would look like afterwards (e.g if we go this route it seems like we need a `CLike` structure, and generalize the whole theory of complex C*-algebras to C*-algebras over a `CLike` field?)

payload.author: thorimur
payload.body:
This looks good to me, thanks. :)

I think maybe there should be a core issue about preresolved names in syntax quotations not recording shake dependencies, unless this has been discussed before? Usually Lean knows that these names are meant to refer to those lemmas in the course of elaborating the meta code, and so during that elaboration and/or checking the meta code it should probably record an extra mod use from these declarations. (We don't need to mention it in this PR, to be clear.)

Not sure if there should be one for the initializer? I'd think maybe a reverse mod use, but perhaps that's too aggressive? (Has this been discussed on zulip?)

More generally I wonder if we should have something like
```lean4
module

public meta import Lean

open Lean Elab Command

syntax (name := shakeRecord) "shake_record " ("public" <|> "private") ("meta" <|> "runtime") ("indirect")? ident* : command

elab_rules : command
| `(command| shake_record $publicOrPrivate $metaOrRuntime $[indirect%$indirectTk?]? $ids*) => do
  let ids ← liftCoreM <| ids.mapM realizeGlobalConstNoOverloadWithInfo
  let isExporting ← match publicOrPrivate.raw[0].getAtomVal with
    | "public"    => pure true
    | "private" => pure false
    | _ => throwUnsupportedSyntax
  let isMeta ← match metaOrRuntime.raw[0].getAtomVal with
    | "meta"    => pure true
    | "runtime" => pure false
    | _ => throwUnsupportedSyntax
  withExporting (isExporting := isExporting) do
    for id in ids do
      recordExtraModUseFromDecl id isMeta
      if indirectTk?.isSome then
        recordIndirectModUse "manual" id
```
so that we could actually manually tell shake that these *declarations* were being used, which would be more stable than import annotations if those declarations ever moved around. But this is fine for now :)

payload.author: D-Thomine
payload.body:
Thanks for your PR!

I'd like to draw your attention to [Set.indicator](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Algebra/Notation/Indicator.html#Set.indicator): `charVec (K := K) s` is equal to `s.indicator (1 : α → K)`. Is there a reason you need this new construction? If not, you are probably better off using already established objects; for instance, your proposition `h` in the proof of `charVec_dotProduct_charVec` is already in the library under the name [Set.inter_indicator_one](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Algebra/GroupWithZero/Indicator.html#Set.inter_indicator_one).

I'll let other people weight on the linear algebra and combinatorics.

payload.body:
> Can you justify why we should add this definition now given that we have done just fine without it for nine years?

I always perceived this as obviously missing API for a basic concept.

Besides that, I can give only vague justifications. I used it in the polyhedral project and found it to be useful. E.g. stating that an affine map is constant is not as convenient with existing API as stating that a linear map is constant. The latter would be constant zero, whereas the former has no specified value.

I made this PR in the expectation that someone would give me a good reasons for why this is a bad idea. So far no one objected. So my impression is that it would not hurt, especially since the use case is clearly separated from `Function.const`.

payload.author: github-actions
payload.body:
### 🚨 PR Title Needs Formatting
Please update the title to match our [commit style conventions](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/commit.html).

Errors from script:
```
labels are [t-topology]
error: the PR title starts with a space
```

<details>
<summary>Details on the required title format</summary>

The title should fit the following format:
```
<kind>(<optional-scope>): <subject>
```
`<kind>` is:

- `feat` (feature)
- `fix` (bug fix)
- `doc` (documentation)
- `style` (formatting, missing semicolons, ...)
- `refactor`
- `test` (when adding missing tests)
- `chore` (maintain)
- `perf` (performance improvement, optimization, ...)
- `ci` (changes to continuous integration, repo automation, ...)

`<optional-scope>` is a name of module or a directory which contains changed modules.
This is not necessary to include, but may be useful if the `<subject>` is insufficient.
The `Mathlib` directory prefix is always omitted.
For instance, it could be

- Data/Nat/Basic
- Algebra/Group/Defs
- Topology/Constructions

`<subject>` has the following constraints:

- do not capitalize the first letter
- no dot(.) at the end
- use imperative, present tense: "change" not "changed" nor "changes"
</details>
<!-- Sticky Pull Request CommentPR Title Check -->

payload.author: FrankieNC
payload.body:
> @FrankieNC Thanks for your PR. I appreciate your help with reducing tech debt in Mathlib. Do you think you see a way to teach the deriving handler to "do the right thing"? So that we can continue using `deriving` in situations like this?

So I found a tag, `@[instance_reducible]`, that makes this work whilst keeping the `deriving`, although it does slow down the build times.

From what I understand, the deriving handler unfolds `⨁ i, β i` to `Π₀ i, β i`, finds the `CoeFun` instance there (which is just `⟨DFunLike.coe⟩`), and rebuilds it as an instance for `⨁ i, β i`. When it copies the `coe` field, it checks that `DFunLike.coe : (Π₀ i, β i) → ∀ i, β i` already has the expected type `(⨁ i, β i) → ∀ i, β i`. The check is done at `instances` transparency and `DirectSum` doesn't unfold there, so it fails, and the handler instead makes an auxiliary constant `instCoeFunDirectSumForall._aux_1` to hold the field (the `set_option` was turning this off). So, `x i` now elaborates to `._aux_1 ι β x i`, but the simp lemmas about the coercion are all stated about `DFunLike.coe`, so `simp` can no longer rewrite it.

My understanding of `@[instance_reducible]`, is that it allows the definition to unfold at `instances` transparency, so the check succeeds and the aux is not generated. The derived instance then has the same name and value as the one the `set_option` used to produce:

```lean
instCoeFunDirectSumForall := fun ι β _ => { coe := DFunLike.coe }
```

For `DirectSum` I had to switch `@[implicit_reducible]`, because `implicit` comes after `instances` in the order `reducible < instances < implicit < default`, so the check still failed.

payload.author: grunweg
payload.body:
Hi! Thanks for trying to help; the differential geometry library can definitely use some helping hands.

Historically, I imagined a different proof for this fact, namely proving that local diffeomorphisms have differential with a left inverse and arguing that therefore, they are immersions and submersions. Mathlib has the first part already; the second part is blocked on an application of the inverse function theorem. (See #40643 for the current progress.)
However, that proof only works well under extra conditions (which are mild in practice, but perhaps less convenient to use) --- so I'm coming around to proving this result directly also.

(Details: one needs to assume a Banach manifold, and that f maps tangent vectors to the boundary of its domain to tangent vectors to the boundary of its codomain). While (local) diffeomorphisms usually satisfy this, proving this in full generality is a bit tricky. I know an argument for C⁰ manifolds in finite dimensions, and one for C¹ manifolds, but am not sure about infinite-dimensional C⁰ Banach manifolds.)

As it so happens, I have proven a mostly more general result in #41203 (applying that to the identity, which we know to be an immersion, should yield this PR's result), so I'd rather merge that one. I'm sorry about this duplicate work! (I also wish my PR would have got reviewed faster, but reviewer capacity is limited.)

I have left some comments below, indicating how your code could be improved --- so you can still learn from them (even if this code won't be merged as-is).

I can suggest some differential geometry tasks which need help (and are not conflicting with this), if you prefer.

payload.body: As a general comment, the whole story around immersions and smooth embeddings has been moving quite slowly (because I get pulled away in different directions, and review capacity is scarce). Let's rather discuss and find a useful project that doesn't conflict with in-progress plans!

payload.author: FrankieNC
payload.body:
> Hi! Thanks for trying to help; the differential geometry library can definitely use some helping hands.
> 
> Historically, I imagined a different proof for this fact, namely proving that local diffeomorphisms have differential with a left inverse and arguing that therefore, they are immersions and submersions. Mathlib has the first part already; the second part is blocked on an application of the inverse function theorem. (See #40643 for the current progress.) However, that proof only works well under extra conditions (which are mild in practice, but perhaps less convenient to use) --- so I'm coming around to proving this result directly also.
> 
> (Details: one needs to assume a Banach manifold, and that f maps tangent vectors to the boundary of its domain to tangent vectors to the boundary of its codomain). While (local) diffeomorphisms usually satisfy this, proving this in full generality is a bit tricky. I know an argument for C⁰ manifolds in finite dimensions, and one for C¹ manifolds, but am not sure about infinite-dimensional C⁰ Banach manifolds.)
> 
> As it so happens, I have proven a mostly more general result in #41203 (applying that to the identity, which we know to be an immersion, should yield this PR's result), so I'd rather merge that one. I'm sorry about this duplicate work! (I also wish my PR would have got reviewed faster, but reviewer capacity is limited.)
> 
> I have left some comments below, indicating how your code could be improved --- so you can still learn from them (even if this code won't be merged as-is).
> 
> I can suggest some differential geometry tasks which need help (and are not conflicting with this), if you prefer.

No worries! Thanks for the review! I was just looking for things to do in the `Wanted` folder. We can close this PR. I can try my hand at a different problem!

payload.author: justin-palumbo
payload.body:
> Wouldnt it make more sense to prove that result, and derive that gdelta subset of polish spaces are polish as a corollary?

I'm not exactly following the reasoning. We're given a Polish space X, and a Gdelta subset Y of X, and we want to conclude that Y is Polish in the subspace topology. I'm not sure how knowing that X is homeomorphic to a subspace of the Hilbert cube, even a Gdelta one, helps establish that Y is Polish.

Perhaps you mean that we could first prove the fact "Gdelta subsets of Hilbert space are Polish" first [a specific instance of the theorem I'm proving here], and then transport the relative Gdelta-ness back and forth between X and Hilbert cube while leveraging exists_embedding_to_hilbert_cube in between. My pushback on that would be I think it's strictly more work (code and mathematically machinery) --- the proof that Gdelta subsets of Hilbert cube are Polish, is the same proof as the general case, and then you're paying extra work for transporting back and forth between spaces.

payload.author: justin-palumbo
payload.body: [btw: am/was planning to formalize the converse direction of this result, that all Polish subspaces of a Polish space are Gdelta --- this is sometimes called Alexandrov's theorem --- that together with https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Topology/MetricSpace/PiNat.html#Metric.PiNatEmbed.exists_embedding_to_hilbert_cube will give Property 4 from wikipedia as a corollary ]

payload.author: felixpernegger
payload.body:
Sorry, I didnt think about this carefully. I had thought the converse holds (i.e. every subset of Hilbert cube is polish).
If it really is the same proof, there is of course no reason to first prove the precific result

payload.author: bfrederick18
payload.body:
Thanks, that makes complete sense. I've pushed a rewrite.

AM-HM is now the general statement, in Finset form: `(#s)^2 ≤ (∑ i ∈ s, z i) * (∑ i ∈ s, (z i)⁻¹)`, with Nesbitt as a corollary of the three-term case. Typeclasses are now `[Semifield R] [LinearOrder R] [IsStrictOrderedRing R] [ExistsAddOfLE R]`.

Working through it, your two suggestions turned out to be linked. Without subtraction the differences can't be formed, so the difference-of-squares script isn't available at all and the proof had to be rebuilt regardless. `two_mul_le_add_sq` is the natural replacement: dividing it by `x * y` gives `2 ≤ x / y + y / x`, and summing that over a Finset is essentially all of AM-HM.

I kept the equality case but had to leave it at `Field` generality, since its certificate is a sum-of-squares identity.

The file is now `Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Field/AmHm.lean` and `Nesbitt.lean` is removed. I put it under `Algebra` rather than `Analysis` since nothing here needs `log`/`exp`, but happy to move it if you'd rather.

On #19414: would you prefer to revive that and have me close this, or shall I keep going here? Either is fine by me :)

(I also think the Lint style job failed on a 503 fetching elan, not on the file.)

payload.author: bfrederick18
payload.body:
Ok a quick update: AM-HM now has its equality criterion plus the two- and three-term specializations, so tb65536's points are all in.

On Nesbitt I've gone in a little cirlce... I removed it after tb65536's comment, then saw vihdzp's and restored it, so the commit log shows both. It's in at the moment, as a short corollary of the three-term case, with its equality case alongside.

The equality criteria did have to move to a field rather than a semifield: each one reduces to `(x - y) ^ 2 = 0` and so needs subtraction. The inequalities are unchanged at semifield generality.

@vihdzp and still wondering about #19414 but no stress

payload.author: bfrederick18
payload.body: -awaiting-author

payload.author: bfrederick18
payload.body:
Oh and one more update, and a correction to what this PR claims.

AM-HM turned out to be `Finset.sq_sum_div_le_sum_sq_div` (Sedrakyan's lemma, already in Mathlib) with every numerator set to 1, at exactly the same typeclasses. I'd missed it because the declaration is named descriptively rather than after Sedrakyan. So `sq_card_le_sum_mul_sum_inv` is now three lines derived from that, instead of the from-scratch induction it was.

That shifts what's actually new here. The inequalities are largely repackaging of what's already there; the part I can't find prior art for is the equality criteria, like Mathlib seems to have this whole family of inequalities without an equality case anywhere.

Which raises a question: would you want the equality criterion for `sq_sum_div_le_sum_sq_div` itself, i.e. equality iff `f i / g i` is constant, rather than just the AM-HM specialization I have? Happy to add it if it's wanted.

I guess the following approach also works? And this method does not need any extra imports.
```
@[fun_prop]
theorem Real.hasTemperateGrowth_sin :
    Real.sin.HasTemperateGrowth := by
  refine ⟨Real.contDiff_sin, fun n ↦ ⟨0, 1, fun x ↦ ?_⟩⟩
  simpa [norm_iteratedFDeriv_eq_norm_iteratedDeriv] using Real.abs_iteratedDeriv_sin_le_one n x

@[fun_prop]
theorem Real.hasTemperateGrowth_cos :
    Real.cos.HasTemperateGrowth := by
  refine ⟨Real.contDiff_cos, fun n ↦ ⟨0, 1, fun x ↦ ?_⟩⟩
  simpa [norm_iteratedFDeriv_eq_norm_iteratedDeriv] using Real.abs_iteratedDeriv_cos_le_one n x

@[fun_prop]
theorem Complex.hasTemperateGrowth_exp_I_mul :
    (fun x : ℝ ↦ Complex.exp (x * Complex.I)).HasTemperateGrowth := by
  simp only [Complex.exp_ofReal_mul_I]
  fun_prop
```

> I'm not a fan of this hardcoded exception to our naming conventions, but if we are to uphold it, then this PR is the correct way to go.

I'm a new contributor so just asking so I can understand what is going on better.  Are you referring to the following statement in the [naming conventions](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/naming.html#predicates-as-suffixes): "Most predicates should be added as prefixes."? And the section then goes on to says stuff like Monotone is an exception?  If so, I think I agree with you.

From what I have seen so far, it seems like the naming conventions are often not followed, which seems strange for a math library.  So, I was thinking of updating the linter, but these over-complicated rules make it hard to form a linter rule.  Do you think we should bring it up in Zulip?

payload.author: than4213
payload.body: OK, researched this a bit.  And it seems like in the case of Monotone, over a third of cases follow the rule and not the exception.  So it seems like my PR could be making things worse.  I feel like I don't have a strong enough opinion to commit to this, and will thus close the PR.

payload.author: JovanGerb
payload.body:
Thanks, the PR looks very good! The main change that I think would be good to do if possible is to refactor `isZero` to be pure instead of in `MetaM`. 

Do you think it would make sense to add `norm_rank` as a norm_num extension?

Could you add a test that stress-tests the swap permutations, and that they are composed in the correct order?

The tactic currently doesn't work for e.g. `ℝ`, but it's nice that we'll be able to implement this on top of the current implementation.

I can imagine that the concept of having computational models for certain types is a feature that more tactics may want to use in the future, so it might be worth thinking about how we can have this more general extensibility. But we can also wait with that until there are more such tactics.

I find the naming of "to parse" and "to render" a bit unusual for going between expressions and other data types. But to be honest I'm not actually sure what we usually call them instead. I've seen the vocabulary of "to reify" and "to reflect".

payload.author: Parcly-Taxel
payload.body:
I would prefer convex polytopes to be defined as they are in the `platonic_classification` lean-eval task – Grünbaum's definition as a finite point set equivalent to the extreme points of its own convex hull. (I have removed a non-emptiness condition from the task code as the "empty polytope" is a thing.)
```lean
structure Polytope where
  v : Finset X
  v_eq_extremePoints : (v : Set X) = Set.extremePoints R (convexHull R (v : Set X))
```

> Can you add the reverse direction

That's false, it implies that all chains are finite but not that there's a maximal chain length.

It's true when all maximal chains have the same length, which is the case in every `IsWeak{Upper/Lower}ModularLattice`, such as `Submodule R M`. But we'd have to add such a class first; see also [this comment](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/42556#discussion_r3754433908).

payload.author: ADedecker
payload.body:
@j-loreaux I think we should coordinate here. Note that we have [spectralRadius](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Algebra/Spectrum.html#spectralRadius) and [spectrum.gelfand_formula](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Algebra/GelfandFormula.html#spectrum.gelfand_formula), but the latter only applies for normed algebras over the complex numbers.

I definitely think it would make sense to have a definition for this limit. The safest option is to have both definitions (maybe calling the latter the `gelfandRadius`?). 
Another option would be to follow Bourbaki and get rid of our current definition of `spectralRadius` in favour of this one, but having two definitions is probably fine.

Also, it would be nice to get this whole thing working in the non-unital setting, but I guess we need `PNat` powers for this.

payload.author: bocowgill
payload.body:
Would you consider also using your newly created `mk_unitInterval` in the [existing proof in `CompletelyRegular.lean`](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/e13dd6052c9cd13288ffa9e5ccc13381b812b42f/Mathlib/Topology/Separation/CompletelyRegular.lean#L217-L219)? It currently reconstructs this cardinality result by unfolding `unitInterval` and applying `mk_Icc_real`:
```lean
rw [lift_continuum, ← lift_continuum.{u, 0}, lift_lt,
   ← mk_Icc_real zero_lt_one, ← unitInterval] at hR
 obtain ⟨r, hr⟩ : ∃ r : I, r ∈ Rᶜ := compl_nonempty_of_mk_lt_mk hR
 ```
With the new simp lemma, those two lines can be replaced by:
```lean
 obtain ⟨r, hr⟩ : ∃ r : I, r ∈ Rᶜ :=
   compl_nonempty_of_mk_lt_mk (by simpa using hR)
 ```
I checked that `simpa` handles the universe lifts and rewrites `#unitInterval` using `mk_unitInterval`. This would simplify an existing client and provide a demonstration of the intended use of the new API. 

If you would prefer to keep this PR focused, the cleanup of `CompletelyRegular.lean`could also be done in a separate PR.

### 🚨 PR Title Needs Formatting
Please update the title to match our [commit style conventions](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/commit.html).

Errors from script:
```
labels are []
error: the PR subject `Monotone.convex_lt/convex_gt state the wrong set` should be lowercased
```

<details>
<summary>Details on the required title format</summary>

The title should fit the following format:
```
<kind>(<optional-scope>): <subject>
```
`<kind>` is:

- `feat` (feature)
- `fix` (bug fix)
- `doc` (documentation)
- `style` (formatting, missing semicolons, ...)
- `refactor`
- `test` (when adding missing tests)
- `chore` (maintain)
- `perf` (performance improvement, optimization, ...)
- `ci` (changes to continuous integration, repo automation, ...)

`<optional-scope>` is a name of module or a directory which contains changed modules.
This is not necessary to include, but may be useful if the `<subject>` is insufficient.
The `Mathlib` directory prefix is always omitted.
For instance, it could be

- Data/Nat/Basic
- Algebra/Group/Defs
- Topology/Constructions

`<subject>` has the following constraints:

- do not capitalize the first letter
- no dot(.) at the end
- use imperative, present tense: "change" not "changed" nor "changes"
</details>

payload.author: robin-carlier
payload.body: It seems there is a big problem here: `lake lint` seems to be ignoring the module system! `#lint` works fine, but `lake lint` is flagging things like `Shrink`, which is already `no_expose`'d.

payload.author: JovanGerb
payload.body:
Ah yes I was a bit worried about this. This is something that I had asked for before, because other environment linters like `simpNF` should ideally also participate in the module system.

For now, maybe it would be possible to use some lower level API than `hasExposedBody` to work around this issue?

payload.author: robin-carlier
payload.body:
> For now, maybe it would be possible to use some lower level API than `hasExposedBody` to work around this issue?

I’d be glad to have pointers on how to do this if this is possible. Maybe @thorimur also has some insights here?

payload.author: JovanGerb
payload.body: By the way, I think this should also lint against appearances of `Fintype.ofFinite`. Or do you think that takes it too far?

payload.author: robin-carlier
payload.body:
I understand the idea but I’d say this would take it a bit far (especially if we use `Expr.getUsedConstants` to look for it in arbitrary depth), but hopefully the current design makes it easy to add constants later on if we decide so

Another possible design is to have an attribute `forbid_exposure` to register constants that we want to see linted by this linter

payload.author: JovanGerb
payload.body:
I'm not sure if it makes sense to reserve the `private` keyword for just proofs. In principle, you could want to wrap a definition in `private`, similar to how we can already do this with `unsafe`.

Also, there is already a `private` syntax that can be used when declaring fields of an instance (`... := private ...`), which I think works for proofs and values.

payload.author: thorimur
payload.body:
Maybe...but I do think we want to be able to have something that is dedicated to proofs and performs the wrapping that `by exact` does in the same circumstances but in a more readable way.

The argument for the current design might look like this: I claim that proofs are qualitatively different when it comes to to wrapping them in aux decls thanks to proof irrelevance, and that wrapping a non-proof is correspondingly a bigger deal (and you should use `private_decl%` or an aux definition to signal this). Structure instance fields are a bit of an outlier since each field is more like a separate body.

The argument against is what you said; it's inconsistent. :) 

Maybe either (1) the error message should point to `private_decl%` or (2) this should be called `private_proof`(`%`).

(EDIT: I've tentatively done (1), at least.)

payload.author: JovanGerb
payload.body: I think I would prefer (2) because of how general the word `private` is, and it seems unreasonable to restrict it to only proofs. If you're looking to have a short name, we could potentially just call it `proof%`.

payload.author: thorimur
payload.body:
After thinking about it a bit, I do worry that it might become very easy to "hold it wrong" if `private` could be used without error for non-proofs. You don't want to make it so that bad decisions are too easy to make. I'm worried that "I'll just fix this unknown identifier error by putting `private` on there" *should* really only work for proofs (if anything), because they *do* behave qualitatively differently than terms.

This is to say that I think it actually is reasonable to disallow `private` for non-proofs 🙃 But that's not to say we should allow it for proof terms, if only because the ubiquity will make people think you should be able to write it everywhere. So my concern about `private` for non-proofs is compatible with both `private`-just-for-proofs and something-else-just-for-proofs (no `private` elaborator at all) 😁

payload.author: wwylele
payload.body:
Can / should this be generalized to more types? What I have in mind is something like
```
def HasNaturalDensity {a : Type a} (A : Set a) {f : Filter (Finset a)) (δ : ℝ) : Prop :=
  Tendsto (fun s : Finset a ↦ ((s.filter (· ∈ A)).card : ℝ) / s.card) f (𝓝 δ)
```
(`Filter (Finset a)` might be also written as `SummationFilter a` as there seems to be an analog of conditional vs unconditional filters)

payload.author: shaikidris
payload.body: Thank you much for the quick response. I’ll check Mathlib’s existing filters on finite subsets and summation conventions, then determine whether the generic notion should be primary, a separate HasDensityAlong because it can change the mathematical meaning of natural density.

payload.author: shaikidris
payload.body:
Ok, I was thinking to model API like this, 

Add generic 
```
def HasDensity (A : Set α) (δ : ℝ) (L : SummationFilter α) : Prop :=
  Tendsto with similar finite subset. 
```

and then the specialized HasNaturalDensity composing this?

```
def HasNaturalDensity (A : Set ℕ) (δ : ℝ) : Prop :=
  HasDensity A δ (SummationFilter.conditional ℕ) ,
``` 
this seems simpler to me.

payload.author: wwylele
payload.body: That looks good to me, though admittedly I am not familiar with this area, so my questions were also for other reviewers to see whether it makes sense

payload.author: b-mehta
payload.body:
I'd much rather have upper/lower density defined very closely with this one. See eg https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/main/FormalConjecturesForMathlib/Data/Set/Density.lean

It may also be worth thinking about relative density at this stage, as that's an important generalisation here. 
I'm not sure if it makes sense to have summation filters here.

Please also use the # notation for finset cardinality.

Can you speak to the use of AI in this pull-request? A number of the proofs here appear to be LLM-generated without human review.

payload.author: shaikidris
payload.body:
1. Thanks for guiding me on this. I was focusing more on generic software API design instead of Mathematical API design. That also makes me now feel if adding lower, upper, relative, etc variants density should be good enough without having to carry the filter-parametric layer.
2. I am using the mathlib style guide and not sure if # notation is mandated, as I see mix of .card also. Nonetheless will add to my local lint-style
3. The requirement, design and stub are from me, but LLM-generated overrode substantially. Also when I raised PR I added the LLM-generated comment in the template but it did not generate the label. Irrespective, adding explicit comment now.

payload.body: @adomani, is there actually a use case for only locally adding a tactic as an allowed tactic? I would think that if a tactic is allowed to be unused, then this should also be so in imported files. payload.author: adomani
payload.body:
I do not have a *strong* reason, but, when I teach, I sometimes like to make the distinction that in some places `done` is not flagged, but when I am polishing the code, I would like it to be flagged.

I would say that for mathlib itself, there is no need for the distinction, but there are many consumers downstream of mathlib that it is probably a good idea to allow local and global silencing to be separate.

payload.author: wwylele
payload.body: Instead of deprecating them, can we change them to the correct statement right away?

payload.author: attilavjda
payload.body:
> Instead of deprecating them, can we change them to the correct statement right away?

One reason I know of for waiting a deprecation cycle before repurposing these lemmas is that they might have callers outside Mathlib, and fixing them results in new lemmas, so if we fix them now those callers will use a different lemma than intended without their users knowing about the change.

payload.author: j-loreaux
payload.body:
> Instead of deprecating them, can we change them to the correct statement right away?

Yes, this is what needs to happen instead. If we deprecate them, then in 6 months they will be automatically removed, and the lemmas will simply be missing. It might break something downstream, but we don't have the tools to address that right now.

payload.author: attilavjda
payload.body:
> > Instead of deprecating them, can we change them to the correct statement right away?
> 
> Yes, this is what needs to happen instead. If we deprecate them, then in 6 months they will be automatically removed, and the lemmas will simply be missing. It might break something downstream, but we don't have the tools to address that right now.

For example `rpow_le_of_le_log` is a duplicate and it's name suggests a different statement, so changing the statement now would result in a new lemma, and callers using the name will use the new lemma without knowing about the change. Deleting the lemma now might allow someone to add the new lemma with the same name sometime after, so it's callers again might use the new lemma with the old name without knowing about the change. Deprecating it records the change, and allows users to know about the change, and since there is no clear need for the upgraded statement, maybe it doesn't have to be added, only deleted, but then the deprecation message seems useful.

payload.author: robin-carlier
payload.body:
Currently, the linter breaks on things like
```lean
variable {α : Type*} [PartialOrder α] [SuccOrder α]
  (succ : ∀ a, ¬IsMax a → motive (succ a))
```

because the `Command.runTermElabM` runs after the elaboration of the `variable` command, so that at the linter step, `succ` is elaborated as the variable defined here, and is not well-typed anymore. There is probably a way to avoid this by being a bit hacky (e.g., counting how many things the currently-linted `variable` command adds to the scope, then dropping them from the scope before running `runTermElabM`). The other possibility is to decide that such variable commands should be fixed, e.g.

```lean
variable [PartialOrder α] [SuccOrder α]
  (succ : ∀ a, ¬IsMax a → motive (Order.succ a))
```

and leave the linter as is.

In #42591 an LLM got Mathlib lint-free with this linter and that speeds the library by 317G instructions/ .22%, which is nice, but also not as dramatic as what #32842 did, it’s also not clear how costly this linter is if active globally (and it’s also assuming the LLM-generated diff did not secretely monomorphize some declarations).

Thanks for the comments! I made the following changes in addition to direct code suggestions:

- Change all instances `[Fact (Prime p)]` into hypotheses `hp : p.Prime`
- Add the easier direction to form iff statements for the IsSquare theorems for `Nat`, `Int`, and `Rat`
- Move the `Rat` statements a block below because the easier direction uses `padicValRat.mul` in the same file
- Add the theorem `padicValNat.dvd_of_ne_zero` to prevent use of `mt`

### 🚨 PR Title Needs Formatting
Please update the title to match our [commit style conventions](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/commit.html).

Errors from script:
```
labels are []
error: the PR title should be of the form
  kind: subject
or
  kind(scope): subject
Allowed values for `kind` are [feat, chore, perf, refactor, style, fix, doc, test, ci]
```

<details>
<summary>Details on the required title format</summary>

The title should fit the following format:
```
<kind>(<optional-scope>): <subject>
```
`<kind>` is:

- `feat` (feature)
- `fix` (bug fix)
- `doc` (documentation)
- `style` (formatting, missing semicolons, ...)
- `refactor`
- `test` (when adding missing tests)
- `chore` (maintain)
- `perf` (performance improvement, optimization, ...)
- `ci` (changes to continuous integration, repo automation, ...)

`<optional-scope>` is a name of module or a directory which contains changed modules.
This is not necessary to include, but may be useful if the `<subject>` is insufficient.
The `Mathlib` directory prefix is always omitted.
For instance, it could be

- Data/Nat/Basic
- Algebra/Group/Defs
- Topology/Constructions

`<subject>` has the following constraints:

- do not capitalize the first letter
- no dot(.) at the end
- use imperative, present tense: "change" not "changed" nor "changes"
</details>
