payload.author: Vierkantor
payload.body:
I think standardising on one form is a great idea! In fact, I'd like one of [`neg_div`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Algebra/Ring/Basic.html#neg_div)/[`neg_div'`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Algebra/Ring/Basic.html#neg_div') to be marked as `@[simp]`.

But I am not convinced right now that `-a / b` is better than `-(a / b)` as a normal form. Here are some arguments against `-a / b`:

* Looking at right hand sides for rewrite lemmas in [Algebra.Ring.Basic](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Algebra/Ring/Basic.html#one_div_neg_eq_neg_one_div), `-(a / b)` seems more popular. This is a weak argument, since no relevant theorem there is marked `@[simp]`.
* `-a / b` is asymmetric in a and b.
* `simp` gets stuck on `-a / b` where it doesn't on `-(a / b)` (as can be seen in the diff). This is the strongest argument against `-a / b` IMO.

Here are some arguments against `-(a / b)`:

* `-(a / b)` has more parentheses.
* `-a / b` is the [internal representation of `Rat.neg`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Init/Data/Rat/Basic.html#Rat.neg).

If we add more `simp` lemmas for `-a / b` then I can be convinced that `-a / b` is a good normal form. (A good way to find out which ones are missing is to make `neg_div'` a `@[simp]` lemma and see what breaks!)

payload.author: SnirBroshi
payload.body:
> but didn't find docs explaining it

Unfortunately it seems that there aren't any, other than [this](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Logic/Basic.html#LibraryNote.decidable_arguments) but it's not very illuminating.

Basically a `[DecidableEq α]` hypothesis is asking for an *algorithm* to determine when two values of type `α` are equal. However since we're using classical logic, every type has such an algorithm.
If the statement of your theorem doesn't use the algorithm, but the proof does, there's no reason to ask the user of the theorem to provide such an algorithm; of course they could also use classical logic to conjure up any algorithm, but that should be the responsibility of your proof.

On the other hand, if you have a statement which does use the algorithm, for example [`Finset.mem_union`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Data/Finset/Lattice/Basic.html#Finset.mem_union) which needs an equality algorithm in order to compute the union of two sets (to discard duplicates), then you might ask why not also use classical logic to conjure up an algorithm and use it in the statement?
```lean
open scoped Classical in -- this automatically uses classical logic whenever `DecidableEq` is needed
theorem Finset.mem_union' {α : Type*} {s t : Finset α} {a : α} : a ∈ s ∪ t ↔ a ∈ s ∨ a ∈ t := by
  simp
```

The answer is that users might have their own custom `DecidableEq α` for their type (e.g. `Nat` & `Bool` have one) and they might want to use your theorem, but you've only proven it for `Finset` unions that use the other algorithm and not "for any `DecidableEq α` algorithm, ...".

See also [diamonds](https://leanprover-community.github.io/glossary.html#diamond).

Did this help? Maybe we can refine this into docs

payload.author: wwylele
payload.body: Is it possible to link hasseDeriv to iterated [Derivation](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/RingTheory/Derivation/Basic.html#Derivation), then prove the multiplication formula there?  (I haven't check thoroughly how much of this is already done)

payload.author: mo271
payload.body:
> Is it possible to link hasseDeriv to iterated [Derivation](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/RingTheory/Derivation/Basic.html#Derivation), then prove the multiplication formula there? (I haven't check thoroughly how much of this is already done)

Good idea. I gave that a try in 
https://github.com/mo271/mathlib4/commits/higher_derivative/

Basically following `Derivation`, i.e. having `leibniz'` as part of the data:

```lean
structure HigherDerivation (R : Type*) (A : Type*) [Semiring R] [Semiring A]
    [Module R A] where
  /-- The family of `R`-linear maps. -/
  toLinearMap : ℕ → (A →ₗ[R] A)
  /-- The zeroth component is the identity. -/
  protected map_zero' : toLinearMap 0 = LinearMap.id
  /-- The image of `1` under each higher component is `0`. -/
  protected map_one' (n : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) : toLinearMap n 1 = 0
  /-- The divided Leibniz rule. -/
  protected leibniz' (n : ℕ) (a b : A) :
    toLinearMap n (a * b) = ∑ ij ∈ antidiagonal n, toLinearMap ij.1 a * toLinearMap ij.2 b
```

However, this does not seem to eliminate the need to proof the Leibniz rule for the instance `LaurentSeries`, which is done in this pull request, right?
Because if we want to then contruct a `HigherDerivation` we will need to supply `leibniz'`, which I'm doing in the linked branch.

I think the proposed link to `hasseDeriv` to a (yet to be defined) iterated Derivation doesn't free us from actually proving the leibniz rule, and is rather follow up work than a prerequisite of the current pull request?

payload.author: wwylele
payload.body:
Sorry, I didn't mean defining a new structure for HigherDerivation.

Deivation itself should be able give the formula for applying iterated deriv on mul. Yoi can then show that LaurentSeries.hasseDeriv is equal to iterated Derivation up to a factor, thus the multiplication formula can tranafer

payload.author: mo271
payload.body:
> Sorry, I didn't mean defining a new structure for HigherDerivation.
> 
> Deivation itself should be able give the formula for applying iterated deriv on mul. Yoi can then show that LaurentSeries.hasseDeriv is equal to iterated Derivation up to a factor, thus the multiplication formula can tranafer

I looked into deriving this from the iterated derivation rule, but there's a characteristic $p$ issue! Transferring the formula from derivative^[k] works in characteristic zero where we can divide by $k!$, but fails in positive characteristic where $k!$ can vanish.

Because `hasseDeriv` works as a divided power derivative even when $k! = 0$, we cannot deduce $A = B$ from $k! \cdot A = k! \cdot B$. To bypass this using a torsion-free trick (if even possible?!), we'd have to prove it over $\mathbb{Z}$ and then use a universal coefficient lift (like `MvPolynomial R ℤ`) because `HahnSeries.map (Int.castRingHom R)` isn't surjective for arbitrary rings. Given the massive amount of boilerplate that would require for Laurent series, doing the finite sum manipulation directly on the coefficients (as currently done in this PR) seems to be the most straightforward and mathematically robust way.

payload.author: eric-wieser
payload.body:
@slamdunktiger, undisclosed AI involvement aside, this is not in its current form anywhere near appropriate for mathlib:
* You have entirely overwritten the mathlib lakefile
* You have tried to set up an entirely unrelated CI
* Your code does not live in the `Mathlib` folder

Attempting to fix the build errors is entirely futile; fundamentally the structure of this PR doesn't make any sense.

I would recommend you host a "Geometry" library on your own person GitHub, and then start a Zulip thread about contributing contributing a small handful of lemmas to mathlib, rather than the whole project at once. That contribution can be in a new PR

If you are using an AI or _are_ an AI, then it is vital that you disclose this when making that post.

If I'm understanding correctly the reason we have poor performance is because the "Strict -> Non-strict" route interacts badly with "IsCancelMul" in the sense that every time we have "Non-strict" now we get "Non-strict -> Strict -> IsCancel + Non-strict". 

Or in the code `MulLeftMono` -> `MulLeftStrictMono` -> `IsCancelMul` + `MulLeftMono` which is a loop. 

I can try to deactivate the `IsLeftCancelMul` instances and see what happens. 

Edit: actually I don't think I was understanding correctly! The problem has more to do with the fact that "strict -> non-strict" adds a bunch of paths which take a long time when instance search fails. Cycles are bad but perhaps not as bad as just having all these failed paths is what I'm understanding right now [according to this Claude gist report](https://gist.github.com/homeowmorphism/acb31705e661b12a63cad18aa00e549b).

## Pull request overview This PR introduces a new style linter (`ellipsisPlaceholders`) that detects function applications ending in a long run of trailing `_` placeholders and suggests replacing them with `..`, along with a dedicated test suite and wiring the linter into Mathlib’s linter imports. **Changes:** - Added `Mathlib.Tactic.Linter.EllipsisPlaceholders`: a syntax/infotree-based linter that validates and suggests rewriting trailing `_ _ …` to `..` when safe. - Added `MathlibTest/Linter/EllipsisPlaceholders.lean` to exercise expected warnings/non-warnings and rewrite validation. - Updated `Mathlib/Init.lean` to import the new linter, and adjusted a lemma in `NoetherNormalization` to use a more direct integrality lemma. ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 4 out of 4 changed files in this pull request and generated 2 comments. | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | Mathlib/Tactic/Linter/EllipsisPlaceholders.lean | New linter implementation and test helper command for validating bulk rewrites. | | MathlibTest/Linter/EllipsisPlaceholders.lean | New regression / behavior tests for the linter’s warnings and skip cases. | | Mathlib/RingTheory/NoetherNormalization.lean | Small proof refactor using an existing integrality lemma (`.kerLift`). | | Mathlib/Init.lean | Adds the new linter module to the standard linter import set. |
Suppressed comments (1) **Mathlib/Tactic/Linter/EllipsisPlaceholders.lean:526** * `tryLintCandidate` calls `shouldSkipValidation` even though `replacementAllowed` already performs the same check. payload.author: grunweg
payload.body:
Hi! Looking at this PR, the particular motivation is not clear to me. Can you elaborate on this (and also mention this in the PR description)? (In general, the PR description should also describe the *why* of a change, if there's something useful to say.)

In the abstract, removing use of automation is not an improvement --- and I'd rather speed up automation than removing its use. Readability matters, and longer manual proofs when there is "nothing going on" are less clear (to me). Of course, the specifics depend on the particular situation --- so can you say more about why?

payload.author: FrankieNC
payload.body:
> Hi! Looking at this PR, the particular motivation is not clear to me. Can you elaborate on this (and also mention this in the PR description)? (In general, the PR description should also describe the _why_ of a change, if there's something useful to say.)
> 
> In the abstract, removing use of automation is not an improvement --- and I'd rather speed up automation than removing its use. Readability matters, and longer manual proofs when there is "nothing going on" are less clear (to me). Of course, the specifics depend on the particular situation --- so can you say more about why?

Thanks for the review! The goal of this PR was to speed up mathlib by removing `aesop` as it is rather slow and replace it with manual proofs (the same motivation as #42405). However, in this case I could not find an appropriate use of `grind` to replace the `aesop` with. The _speed up_ from using manual proofs is also not very impressive.

I will close this PR.

payload.author: copilot-pull-request-reviewer
payload.body:
## Pull request overview This PR refactors and generalizes lemmas around `IsNonarchimedean`, removing several `FunLike`-style hypotheses and updating downstream call sites to use the new, more direct APIs. **Changes:** - Refactored `Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Ring/IsNonarchimedean.lean` to state results for plain functions `f : α → R` with explicit hypotheses (e.g. neg-invariance, `f 0` minimality) instead of `FunLike`/`*HomClass` assumptions. - Updated multiple Gauss norm / seminorm / spectral norm proofs to use the new dot-notation methods (e.g. `hna.finset_image_add_of_nonempty`, `hna.apply_sum_eq_of_lt`). - Added a small helper lemma `map_zero_le` for nonnegative, zero-preserving hom classes and used it to supply the new explicit hypotheses in updated lemmas. ### Reviewed changes Copilot reviewed 10 out of 10 changed files in this pull request and generated no comments.
Show a summary per file | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | Mathlib/RingTheory/Polynomial/GaussNorm.lean | Switches to new `IsNonarchimedean` finset/sum lemmas in Gauss norm submultiplicativity proofs. | | Mathlib/RingTheory/MvPowerSeries/GaussNorm.lean | Updates `IsNonarchimedean` finset/sum lemma usage in multivariate Gauss norm arguments. | | Mathlib/NumberTheory/Padics/PadicNorm.lean | Adapts `add_eq_max_of_ne` proof to the generalized `IsNonarchimedean` API. | | Mathlib/NumberTheory/NumberField/Completion/FinitePlace.lean | Supplies newly-required explicit hypotheses (`map_zero_le`, `map_one`, `map_neg_eq_map`) to `apply_*Cast_le_one` lemmas. | | Mathlib/NumberTheory/Height/NumberField.lean | Updates integer-cast boundedness proof to match the generalized `apply_intCast_le_one`. | | Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Unbundled/SpectralNorm.lean | Updates to new `IsNonarchimedean` helper lemmas (finset/multiset “dominant term” style arguments). | | Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Unbundled/RingSeminorm.lean | Adjusts `add_pow_le` usage to the new generalized statement. | | Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Unbundled/FiniteExtension.lean | Rewrites finset-dominance steps using new `finset_image_add` API and `map_zero_le`. | | Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Ring/IsNonarchimedean.lean | Core refactor: removes `FunLike`-based assumptions, reorganizes sections, and generalizes multiple statements. | | Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Hom/Basic.lean | Adds `map_zero_le` helper lemma to support the new explicit-minimum hypotheses. |

> Hi! Looking at this PR, the particular motivation is not clear to me. Can you elaborate on this (and also mention this in the PR description)? (In general, the PR description should also describe the _why_ of a change, if there's something useful to say.)
> 
> This PR adds 80 lines of diff... making a number of proofs less readable to me. This needs good justification. While the relative speed-up is impressive, I'm not convinced the absolute numbers make it worth it.

Thanks for the review! My main motivation was to speed up the build times of mathlib. I thought one way to do so was to replace `aesop` with explicit terms or a manual proof. I didn't know that Mathlib's preference is automation over manual proofs, I will keep it mind! So, I reworked the PR to replace (where possible) the use of `aesop` with `grind` which still speeds up the build times of the file.

If your PR does not appear there, it is probably because it is not successfully building (i.e., it doesn't have a green checkmark), has the `awaiting-author` tag, or another reason described in the [Lifecycle of a PR](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/index.html#lifecycle-of-a-pr). payload.author: JovanGerb
payload.body: The fact that `fun_prop` breaks after simplifying the function, seems to suggest that there are missing `fun_prop` tags for the simplified functions. Is that the case?

payload.author: gasparattila
payload.body: The failing proofs were all relying on a `fun_prop` bug, so it's expected that they break. I don't know any place where we really need `fun_prop` without `simp`, however, I could imagine a situation where a continuous function is the composition of non-continuous functions. See [`AddCircle.homeomorphCircle'_symm_apply`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Complex/Circle.html#AddCircle.homeomorphCircle'_symm_apply) for an example, though this doesn't seem to appear anywhere where this `autoParam` is used.

payload.author: JovanGerb
payload.body: Aha, in that case it does seem good to always call simp. And then we can hopefully fix the `fun_prop` bug. What is the bug?

payload.author: gasparattila
payload.body:
See [#mathlib4 > `fun_prop` sometimes unfolds semireducible definitions](https://leanprover.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/287929-mathlib4/topic/.60fun_prop.60.20sometimes.20unfolds.20semireducible.20definitions/with/574596569) for the bug. I plan to use this `fun_prop_simp` tactic for more bundled morphisms (which currently use `:= by fun_prop`) to reduce the number of proofs that rely on this bug.

But I would still keep the `fun_prop` call without `simp`, just in case it may be needed somewhere. I don't think it matters much for performance, since `fun_prop` usually fails fast for goals where we need `simp`.

payload.author: grunweg
payload.body:
I'm worried about the performance implications of making a call to `simp` the default behaviour. One reason we're phasing our `continuity` in favour of `fun_prop` is that the initial `simp_all` step in aesop is too slow. Is always calling simp the right default?

Also, can you document the broader rationale for your change in the PR description? (I don't understand yet how this will remove backward compatibility options. This PR doesn't do this; you could make a follow-up PR demonstrating this.)

payload.author: gasparattila
payload.body:
The benchmark shows that there's no performance difference compared to the currently used `dsimp`.

I believe that this tactic is still much faster than `continuity`, since it calls `simp` just once (`continuity` calls `simp_all` on every subgoal, which itself calls `simp` in a loop on every hypothesis). Another performance issue with `continuity` is the lack of indexing for functions, together with unification at default transparency, which results in many slowly failing unification problems. `fun_prop` avoids most of this slowness (though it still uses default transparency, see #42330 for a fix).

An issue with `dsimp` is that some theorems which hold definitionally aren't tagged with `@[defeq]`. See https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/35548#discussion_r3714800456 for an example where `@[defeq]` had to be added manually. Here, `simps` rewrites using a lemma which holds by defeq in this specific example but not in general. I expect that this will become more common once classes like `IsAddApply` are widely used.

I've temporarily added a log message to find which `backward.defeqAttrib.useBackward` options are removable after this PR. Unfortunately, there's no automation that removes them, so some of them may be already unnecessary.

payload.body:
This works here and fails on master:
```lean
/-- info: Associates.instPreorder.toLE -/
#guard_msgs in
#synth LE (Associates Nat)
```
but it depends on the instance priorities and doesn't really test the issue, e.g. the same test with `Preorder` works on master even though there's a `Preorder` instance for `Quotient`s. We could do:
```lean
attribute [-instance] Associates.instPreorder Associates.instPartialOrder Associates.instLattice

/--
error: failed to synthesize
  LE (Associates ℕ)

Hint: Additional diagnostic information may be available using the `set_option diagnostics true` command.
-/
#guard_msgs in
#synth LE (Associates Nat)
```
but it seems weird.

wdyt?

payload.author: mcdoll
payload.body: You guessed right. I want to refactor `Seminorm.IsBounded` (which is a statement about `SeminormFamily`) to `Seminorm.IsBoundedBy p q` which will mean that there exists a constant C such that `p \leq C q` and then change `Seminorm.IsBounded` accordingly to `SeminormFamily.IsBoundedBy` (with `p := p.comp f`). The point for that is that I want to generalize the extension of linear maps to continuous linear maps to locally convex spaces (or polynormable spaces) and get the normed space version without too much pain. Translating between `WithSeminorms` and `NormedSpace` is a bit awkward at the moment - basically because we implemented `WithSeminorms` after we had normed spaces.

payload.body:
### 🚨 PR Title Needs Formatting
Please update the title to match our [commit style conventions](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/commit.html).

Errors from script:
```
labels are [new-contributor]
error: a PR's scope should be a directory or file name, not a module name
hint: the scope contains a dot, use forward slashes instead
```

<details>
<summary>Details on the required title format</summary>

The title should fit the following format:
```
<kind>(<optional-scope>): <subject>
```
`<kind>` is:

- `feat` (feature)
- `fix` (bug fix)
- `doc` (documentation)
- `style` (formatting, missing semicolons, ...)
- `refactor`
- `test` (when adding missing tests)
- `chore` (maintain)
- `perf` (performance improvement, optimization, ...)
- `ci` (changes to continuous integration, repo automation, ...)

`<optional-scope>` is a name of module or a directory which contains changed modules.
This is not necessary to include, but may be useful if the `<subject>` is insufficient.
The `Mathlib` directory prefix is always omitted.
For instance, it could be

- Data/Nat/Basic
- Algebra/Group/Defs
- Topology/Constructions

`<subject>` has the following constraints:

- do not capitalize the first letter
- no dot(.) at the end
- use imperative, present tense: "change" not "changed" nor "changes"
</details>
<!-- Sticky Pull Request CommentPR Title Check -->

> I tried quite a bit to simplify the proof, as the <;> block is annoying. However this led to the proof blowing up in size (i.e. mre than doubling in size). Thus the proof (except the minor suggestions i gave) is likely good as is.

Amusingly, you may have more-or-less reverse engineered the original (AI-generated) proof!  Here was what the AI gave me before I did a large round of golfing:
```
open scoped Real in
/-- Euler's reflection formula for the digamma function: 
`ψ (1 - s) = ψ s + π * cot (π * s)` for `s` not an integer. -/
theorem digamma_one_sub {s : ℂ} (hs : ∀ n : ℤ, s ≠ n) :
    digamma (1 - s) = digamma s + ↑π * cot (↑π * s) := by
  have hπ : (π : ℂ) ≠ 0 := ofReal_ne_zero.mpr Real.pi_ne_zero
  have hsnat : ∀ m : ℕ, s ≠ -↑m := fun m ↦ by simpa using hs (-m)
  have h1snat : ∀ m : ℕ, (1 : ℂ) - s ≠ -↑m :=
    fun m h ↦ hs (1 + m) (by push_cast; linear_combination -h)
  have hsin : sin (↑π * s) ≠ 0 := fun h ↦ by
    obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := sin_eq_zero_iff.mp h
    exact hs k (mul_left_cancel₀ hπ (hk.trans (mul_comm _ _)))
  have hGs : Gamma s ≠ 0 := Gamma_ne_zero hsnat
  have hG1s : Gamma (1 - s) ≠ 0 := Gamma_ne_zero h1snat
  have hdG1s : DifferentiableAt ℂ (fun z ↦ Gamma (1 - z)) s :=
    (differentiableAt_Gamma (1 - s) h1snat).comp s (by fun_prop)
  have hL : logDeriv (fun z ↦ Gamma (1 - z)) s = -digamma (1 - s) := by
    have hd : deriv (fun z : ℂ ↦ 1 - z) s = -1 := ((hasDerivAt_id s).const_sub 1).deriv
    rw [show (fun z : ℂ ↦ Gamma (1 - z)) = Gamma ∘ fun z ↦ 1 - z from rfl,
      logDeriv_comp (differentiableAt_Gamma _ h1snat) (by fun_prop), hd, ← digamma_def, mul_neg_one]
  have hR : logDeriv (fun z ↦ sin (↑π * z)) s = cot (↑π * s) * ↑π := by
    have hg : HasDerivAt (fun z : ℂ ↦ ↑π * z) ↑π s := by
      simpa using (hasDerivAt_id s).const_mul (↑π : ℂ)
    rw [show (fun z : ℂ ↦ sin (↑π * z)) = sin ∘ fun z ↦ ↑π * z from rfl,
      logDeriv_comp (by fun_prop) hg.differentiableAt, logDeriv_sin, hg.deriv]
  have key := congrArg (logDeriv · s) (funext fun z ↦ Gamma_mul_Gamma_one_sub z)
  rw [logDeriv_mul s hGs hG1s (differentiableAt_Gamma s hsnat) hdG1s, hL,
    logDeriv_div s hπ hsin (by fun_prop) (by fun_prop), logDeriv_const, hR, ← digamma_def] at key
  simp only [Pi.zero_apply, zero_sub] at key
  linear_combination -key
```

payload.author: SnirBroshi
payload.body:
> This is the vertex-extension step underlying greedy coloring, and is the ingredient needed to prove the bound `chromaticNumber ≤ maxDegree + 1`.

This lemma could be nice, but note that the bound is proven in #38357, with a more general form of greedy coloring than it seems you're alluding to.

payload.author: brianrabern
payload.body:
good point. thanks. I'll update the PR description: this lemma is not meant as a route to `χ ≤ Δ + 1` (that's covered more generally in #38357).

The intended use is as a local induction step: if `G - v` is `n`-colourable and `deg(v) < n`, extend the colouring to `G`. That's the form needed later for inductive arguments such as Brooks, rather than a global greedy colouring.

payload.author: SnirBroshi
payload.body:
> That's the form needed later for inductive arguments such as Brooks 

I was hoping my PR would also lead to Brooks, but I haven't thought it through yet

payload.author: brianrabern
payload.body: Brooks needs a Δ-colouring outside the clique / odd-cycle cases, so I expect it still needs a separate structural argument

payload.author: kebekus
payload.body:
Dear @yuanyi-350 

Thank you for your contribution. I agree that a generalization of the mean value property is highly desirable. On the other hand, I am unsure if a generalization to functions on the complex plane with `RCLike` targets is very natural. IMHO, the result should hold for harmonic functions with values in arbitrary Banach spaces. I asked Claude Code for a quick proof; please find the result below. I would be more than glad if you could consider submitting a generalization to that level. Please feel free to use or re-use any of the code below; I do not claim any copyright or intellectual property.

Best,

Stefan.


---
import Mathlib.Analysis.Complex.Harmonic.MeanValue
import Mathlib.Analysis.LocallyConvex.SeparatingDual

/-!
# The Mean Value Property of Vector-Valued Harmonic Functions

The file `Mathlib/Analysis/Complex/Harmonic/MeanValue.lean` establishes the mean value property for
harmonic functions `f : ℂ → ℝ`. Harmonicity is however defined for functions with values in an
arbitrary real normed vector space `F`, and the mean value property holds in that generality, as
soon as `F` is complete. This file proves the generalized statements; they are intended to replace
the real-valued versions in Mathlib.

Completeness of `F` cannot be dropped: `circleAverage` is defined in terms of the Bochner integral,
which is junk (zero) whenever the target space is incomplete.

The proof reduces to the real-valued case. Circle averages commute with continuous linear maps, and
composition with continuous linear maps preserves harmonicity. So `g (circleAverage f c R)` equals
`circleAverage (g ∘ f) c R = g (f c)` for every continuous linear functional `g : F →L[ℝ] ℝ`. Since
continuous linear functionals separate the points of a normed space (Hahn-Banach, in the form of
`SeparatingDual.eq_iff_forall_dual_eq`), this suffices.
-/

open InnerProductSpace Metric Real

namespace InnerProductSpace

/-!
## Compatibility of `HarmonicContOnCl` with Linear Maps
-/

section

variable
  {E : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ E] [FiniteDimensional ℝ E]
  {F : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]
  {G : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup G] [NormedSpace ℝ G]

/--
Compositions of continuous `ℝ`-linear maps with functions that are harmonic on a set and continuous
on its closure are again harmonic on the set and continuous on its closure.
-/
theorem HarmonicContOnCl.comp_CLM {f : E → F} {s : Set E} (h : HarmonicContOnCl f s)
    (l : F →L[ℝ] G) :
    HarmonicContOnCl (l ∘ f) s :=
  ⟨h.1.comp_CLM l, l.continuous.comp_continuousOn h.2⟩

end

/-!
## The Mean Value Property
-/

variable
  {F : Type*} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F] [CompleteSpace F]
  {f : ℂ → F} {c : ℂ} {R : ℝ}

/--
The **Mean Value Property** of harmonic functions: If `f : ℂ → F` is harmonic in a neighborhood of a
closed disc of radius `R` and center `c`, then the circle average `circleAverage f c R` equals
`f c`.
-/
theorem HarmonicOnNhd.circleAverage_eq (hf : HarmonicOnNhd f (closedBall c |R|)) :
    circleAverage f c R = f c := by
  have h : CircleIntegrable f c R :=
    (hf.continuousOn.mono sphere_subset_closedBall).circleIntegrable'
  rw [SeparatingDual.eq_iff_forall_dual_eq (R := ℝ)]
  intro g
  rw [← g.circleAverage_comp_comm h]
  exact _root_.HarmonicOnNhd.circleAverage_eq (hf.comp_CLM g)

/--
The **Mean Value Property** of harmonic functions: If `f : ℂ → F` is harmonic on a disc of radius
`|R|` and center `c` and continuous on its closure, then the circle average `circleAverage f c R`
equals `f c`.
-/
theorem HarmonicContOnCl.circleAverage_eq (hf : HarmonicContOnCl f (ball c |R|)) :
    circleAverage f c R = f c := by
  have h : CircleIntegrable f c R :=
    (hf.continuousOn_ball.mono sphere_subset_closedBall).circleIntegrable'
  rw [SeparatingDual.eq_iff_forall_dual_eq (R := ℝ)]
  intro g
  rw [← g.circleAverage_comp_comm h]
  exact _root_.HarmonicCo

payload.author: MichaelStollBayreuth
AlyciaBHZ
payload.body:
thanks for the review — all applied, though one of them needed an extra step: replacing `set m := (p - 1) / 2` with `obtain ⟨m, hm⟩ := hp` changes what `m` denotes. Under `set` it abbreviates `(p - 1) / 2` and the goal displays it as `m`, whereas the `obtain` gives the witness from `Odd p` with `hm : p = 2 * m + 1`, leaving the goal stated in terms of `(p - 1) / 2`. The two are equal only given `hm`, not definitionally, so the calc block no longer closes:

```
error: Mathlib/NumberTheory/Wilson.lean:52:82: unsolved goals
case calc.step
p m : ℕ
hm : p = 2 * m + 1
⊢ (-1) ^ m * ↑m ! ^ 2 = (-1) ^ ((p - 1) / 2) * ↑((p - 1) / 2)! ^ 2
```

I kept the `obtain` and added `rw [show (p - 1) / 2 = m by lia]` right after it to move the goal across. This has the side benefit that `hm` is now actually used, so the unused hypothesis you flagged is gone either way. If you have a shorter way to do this, I am happy to change it.

payload.body:
I don't have an opinion on whether it's desirable behaviour for `map`. However, if it is implemented, wouldn't it make sense to act at the level of `MeasureTheory.Measure.Map`? e.g. if `f` is not measurable, send all the mass to a single point (i.e. replace `f` by a constant function).

It would also be instructive to see what breaks in `MeasureTheory`, and what has to be adapted. [AEMeasurable.of_map_ne_zero](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/Map.html#AEMeasurable.of_map_ne_zero) is the most obvious to me. It is a weird statement which should probably be removed, but following it, it looks like something might break at [ProbabilityTheory.mgf_dirac](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Probability/Moments/Basic.html#ProbabilityTheory.mgf_dirac). That statement would become false with your new convention, provided that `Measure.map` were replaced by `ProbabilityMeasure.map`, which would make sense in this context. Though an additional measurability hypothesis would fix it; there's a rabbit hole to follow here.

Edit: If both `Measure.map` and `ProbabilityMeasure.map` are used in probabilistic settings, which [ProbabilityTheory.mgf_dirac](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Probability/Moments/Basic.html#ProbabilityTheory.mgf_dirac) suggests, it seems quite important to me to keep both definitions coherent, including with this convention.

payload.author: EtienneC30
payload.body: I don't think we should adapt the definition of `Measure.map`, if only because when the codomain is empty you can't define the map as a Dirac mass. To me this change is merely for convenience when writing `ProbabilityMeasure.map`, the convenience of junk values in non-measurable cases does not really matter to me (btw `mgf_dirac` should be written in terms of `HasLaw`).

payload.author: D-Thomine
payload.body:
> I don't think we should adapt the definition of `Measure.map`, if only because when the codomain is empty you can't define the map as a Dirac mass.

Wait. If the codomain is empty, then the map is trivial and automatically measurable, so you should never fall into the (non-ae-measurable + empty codomain) case, am I wrong? It would make the definition slightly annoying, but anything beyond that should be fine.

> To me this change is merely for convenience when writing ProbabilityMeasure.map, the convenience of junk values in non-measurable cases does not really matter to me (btw mgf_dirac should be written in terms of HasLaw).

I understand the motivation, but different edge-case behaviours for such closely related notions are going to be a (low-scale) headache, and it would be nice to avoid it altogether.

If there is a good motivation to not adopt the proportional-to-Dirac convention in the measurable case, I would also like to know it.

payload.author: EtienneC30
payload.body:
> Wait. If the codomain is empty, then the map is trivial and automatically measurable, so you should never fall into the (non-ae-measurable + empty codomain) case, am I wrong? It would make the definition slightly annoying, but anything beyond that should be fine.

Yes you're right. And we could also turn `isProbabilityMeasure_map` back into an instance... There are results that rely on the current junk value though, I will investigate to see if it is worth it.

payload.author: EtienneC30
payload.body: @D-Thomine I went through several files, adding some measurability hypotheses here and there, until I hit [MeasureTheory.AEStronglyMeasurable.comp_snd_map_prod_id](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Probability/Kernel/Condexp.html#MeasureTheory.AEStronglyMeasurable.comp_snd_map_prod_id). Because of the change I need to show that `id` is `m-mΩ`-ae-measurable, which will require some sort of almost everywhere `mΩ ≤ m` statement, which is not good since we later want to take the conditional expectation w.r.t. `m`. Probably there is a way of bypassing this, but I will stop here.

payload.author: sfingali
payload.body:
Thanks for the review — all three points are correct. I've restructured to match the ContinuousMonoidHom pattern:

- `ContinuousValuation` now `extends Valuation A Γ₀` directly (parent projection `toValuation`, plus `continuous_toValuation`)
- `ContinuousValuationClass` now `extends ValuationClass F A Γ₀, ContinuousMapClass F A Γ₀` — empty body, `map_continuous` inherited
- `toValuationHom` removed (pure duplication of the parent projection)

Builds clean (1412 jobs, no warnings) and passes the mathlib linter set. Pushing the update now.

payload.body:
Hello from triage! Can you comment on whether you used AI for this project? Thanks!
(Per mathlib's [AI policy](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/#use-of-ai), this is not forbidden in principle, but its usage must be disclosed.)

payload.author: AlyciaBHZ
payload.body:
Yes, and apologies for not saying so up front — I should have put it in the description when I opened the PR.

The Lean proofs were drafted by an OpenAI Codex agent, orchestrated by Claude Code. I set the target, the constraints and the API to reuse, and reviewed the result.

Before submitting I ran, by hand rather than trusting the agent's report:

- `lake build Mathlib.Logic.Relation`, `lake exe runLinter Mathlib.Logic.Relation`, `lake exe lint-style Mathlib.Logic.Relation`
- the duplicate search against current `master` rather than a cached checkout — `git grep` over `origin/master` for `newman`, `LocallyConfluent`, `locally_confluent` and local confluence turns up only the historical mention of the name in `Mathlib/Geometry/Manifold/PoincareConjecture.lean` and the free-group specialization `FreeGroup.Red.church_rosser`
- a check that the well-foundedness hypothesis is not redundant, via a four-element relation that is locally confluent but not confluent

The port from our Lean 4.28 development to current master needed one change, `{α : Sort*}` → `{α : Type*}`, since `Join` and `ReflTransGen` are stated for `Type*` here.

I've added the same disclosure to the PR description. I don't have permission to set labels — could you add `LLM-generated`?

Happy to answer questions about any of the three proofs.

payload.author: felixpernegger
payload.body: LLM-generated

payload.author: chenson2018
payload.body:
See also #40368 which is interested in expanding the confluence API. As I explained there, we have these in CSLib ([`Cslib/Foundations/Relation/`](https://github.com/leanprover/cslib/tree/main/Cslib/Foundations/Relation)), sometimes in more generality and with dedicated definitions for concepts like local confluence and termination that make the statements much nicer.

As mentioned on that PR and on Zulip, I'm happy to upstream but wanted confirmation this was material was desired before I spent time. I actually briefly talked with @b-mehta in-person yesterday about this and he seemed to think it'd be reasonable to have in Mathlib, so maybe I should just go ahead and start preparing these PRs?

payload.author: AlyciaBHZ
payload.body:
---

Thanks for pointing at CSLib — I had only searched Mathlib and Batteries, so I missed it
entirely, and that is squarely on me.

Having looked at `Cslib/Foundations/Relation/Confluence.lean`, your version is better than
mine on every axis I care about. `LocallyConfluent.Terminating_toConfluent` is the same
theorem, and `Convergent.unique_Normal` subsumes both of my corollaries. More importantly
you have the named predicates — `LocallyConfluent`, `Terminating`, `SN`, `Normal`,
`Convergent` — which is exactly the layer I decided to leave out on the grounds that there
was no concrete consumer yet. Clearly there is one, and it is yours.

So: please do go ahead. I am happy to close this PR in favour of your upstreaming, and I
would rather Mathlib got the general version than a narrower one that has to be
reconciled later. If it is useful I am glad to review, or to help with any of the
mechanical parts of the port.

One small thing that might be worth keeping, if it does not already have an analogue on
your side: the docstring here spells out that `church_rosser` and Newman's lemma have
incomparable hypotheses — the former assumes a one-step diamond condition and no
termination — since that was the first question I had when I found `church_rosser` in this
file and could not tell whether Newman's lemma was already there in disguise.

payload.author: AlyciaBHZ
payload.body:
Both fair, thanks for taking the time.

The name is wrong — CSLib's `LocallyConfluent.Terminating_toConfluent` is the right shape, describing the statement instead of a person. And the docstring was arguing a comparison rather than saying what the theorem does, which is not what a docstring is for.

Closing this. As @chenson2018 points out above, CSLib already has these results in more generality and with proper named predicates, and he is going to upstream them.

payload.author: vihdzp
payload.body:
It seems to me that there are two main uses of `proof_wanted` at the moment:
- State open problems, using definitions from the file that they're in.
- State future developments related to the file that they're in.

In the first case, it seems weird to say that we "want these results in Mathlib"; we don't even know if they're true or not! In the second case, it seems useful to keep the `proof_wanted`s where they already are, since the presumption is that they can be proven with the surrounding material.

I do think the idea of a `Wanted` directory is a good one (we can sketch out developments before putting them in Mathlib), but I'm not sure if the `proof_wanted`s we have right now indiscriminately belong in said directory.

payload.author: kbuzzard
payload.body:
Part of the reason for this push is a sense of unease which some of us have, because of the tension between "mathlib is sorry-free" and "hmm, here are some statements in mathlib which seem to have no proofs and might not even be true". The philosophy is "move all such things into a new place which is called `Wanted` so it's clearer what is going on". 

My vision is that we can have comments in mathlib saying "we want X,Y,Z for (insert reason here), see `Wanted.Path.To.This.File`". 

Probably this PR merits a wider discussion but I still have not read it through myself (I will try and prioritise it) and I don't want to un-WIP it yet until I am happy to stand by it (currently it's LLM-generated so goodness knows what's in it). It's probably sensible to wait until I've read it through before we start a discussion on the public Zulip so we minimise noise.

> This looks good. I wonder though, since you have been looking at this kind of stuff, would it be more natural for `lt_top_iff_one_lt` (which is used in the proof), to be `ne_top_iff_one_lt` instead?
> 
> VSCode search indicates `ne_top` is somewhat more common than `lt_top`. Maybe there ought to be some convention (or maybe there is which i dont know about...)

There is https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/style.html#normal-forms, which suggests that `≠ ∞` is more useful in assumptions while `< ∞` is more useful in conclusions. As for `lt_top_iff_one_lt `, there exists its sibling `ne_top_iff_ne_one` and it's easy to use `_.lt_top` or `_.ne`, so I think everything is fine here?

payload.author: raoxiaojia
payload.body:
I've assessed #38596 -- my first impression is that the 2 PRs are largely complementary despite apparently mentioning the same pivot/echelon form definition. If I read correctly, ~2/3 of LOC in #38596 is for defining equivalence via row operations by GL-actions, which would be a useful bridge to the transvection defs regardless of which definition of pivots/echelon form is used.

For the concrete definition of pivots and echelon form, I do prefer this version though, for several reasons:
- I think it's valuable to have the entire pivot set/map of the matrix itself as an explicit object (`IsPivotedBy` in this PR), especially since it's an important interface for the computational tactic later. The existential-based def of row-echelon in #38596 at `row_zero_or_pivot` makes it harder to use for pivot-related computations (which the rank tactic needs later).
- The totalised pivot entry (`IsLeadingEntry` in this PR vs `IsPivot` in the previous PR) is more convenient to use and keep the definition compact (instead of needing separate considerations for zero-rows).
- This PR actually derives the several fields in `IsEchelonForm` as corollaries from the pivot map (`IsPivotedBy.monotone` and `isPivotedBy_iff` -- in particular the latter is an alternate formulation of echelon form that is close to what the previous stated as their echelon form def).
- I actually considered a formulation similar to that PR for the `IsRowEchelon` def as well, but I ultimately thought the version here is more idiomatic due to existing similar shapes of BlockTriangular formulation.
- The typeclasses assumed are generally weaker in this PR, although I agree that most people are perhaps content with the indices having a linear order.

Of course, I can't be perfectly unbiased here (although I'm trying to) given that I wrote this PR, so I'm happy to receive comments from the others as well.

payload.author: raoxiaojia
payload.body: One thing I forgot to say in above after reading the previous PR -- I think the 'pivot' usually refers to the entry instead of the entire set of entries, so I might want to rename stuff in this PR as well (eg `isLeadingEntry` can become `isPivotEntry` or sth).

payload.author: thorimur
payload.body:
This looks good to me, thanks! :)

I've gone through bit by bit and reviewed each change, using the "viewed" github feature to keep track of progress. I've
1. made sure that variables were indeed only removed, and not changed or added
2. tried to make sure no unusual whitespace was introduced through removal (but did not insist on cleaning up existing unusual whitespace)

I found no instances of violating (1.). My comments just take care of (2.) when I caught it.

One possible objection to this PR is that those variables show what is *allowed* to be available in these sections for future lemmas, and so should not necessarily be removed. I think incorrectly suggesting that they *are* used when they're not is worse than what we lose in that way, though, and so this PR is worth it.

payload.author: seewoo5
payload.body: @loefflerd @CBirkbeck Could you take a look? Also, I found that weight 4 and 6 Eisenstein series are denoted (abbreviated) as `E₄` and `E₆`, while weight 2 Eisenstein series is denoted as `E2`. Would it be better to make notations consistent?

payload.author: loefflerd
payload.body:
Random remarks at first glance:

- Notating E2 with a subscript sounds sensible, but it would probably mean lots of deprecations and general churn; I'm not sure it's worth the small benefit now that those names are already in mathlib.

- I don't think "RamanujanFormula" is a good module name; Ramanujan had _many_ formulas besides these.

payload.author: seewoo5
payload.body:
> Random remarks at first glance:
> 
> * Notating E2 with a subscript sounds sensible, but it would probably mean lots of deprecations and general churn; I'm not sure it's worth the small benefit now that those names are already in mathlib.
> * I don't think "RamanujanFormula" is a good module name; Ramanujan had _many_ formulas besides these.

- I see - I totally agree with you.
- One possibility is to merge whole file into `Derivative.lean` (keep namespace `Derivative`), which seems fine considering that total # of lines will be around 500. Otherwise I don't have good alternative name for module now...

payload.author: loefflerd
payload.body:
> > * I don't think "RamanujanFormula" is a good module name; Ramanujan had _many_ formulas besides these.

> * One possibility is to merge whole file into `Derivative.lean` (keep namespace `Derivative`), which seems fine considering that total # of lines will be around 500. Otherwise I don't have good alternative name for module now...

We could do this. I also overlooked before that `RamanujanFormula` is living inside `EisensteinSeries` so there is less of an issue about confusion with other formulae due to Ramanujan, so it would also be ok as it is I guess.

payload.author: seewoo5
payload.body: Thanks, then I may keep as-is for now. Also, the current CI error looks quite random for me - probably it may dissappear for future commits?

payload.author: CBirkbeck
payload.body: Yeah I agree with David, it might be more pain than its worth renaming E2. This also means we can keep the subscript for actual modular forms and E2 can stay a not-quite modular form
